text: Africa is not one place. It has 54 UN member states, about 1.5 billion people and over 2,000 languages. It has had empires, city-states, trading networks, universities and religions that shaped the world, and it suffered centuries of slave trades and decades of colonial rule.

For a long time outsiders told Africa’s story for it. In 1963 an Oxford professor said Africa had no history, only the history of Europeans in Africa. That claim was wrong, and this deep dive shows the evidence: archaeology, genetics, African written records and oral traditions, as well as European ones.

Early hominins appear in Africa. “Lucy”, a 3.2-million-year-old Australopithecus skeleton found in Ethiopia in 1974, walked upright with a small, ape-sized brain. Homo erectus, the first to spread beyond Africa, appears about 1.9 million years ago.
Once controversial, the African origin of the human lineage is now accepted worldwide; in the early 1900s many European scientists expected to find it in Asia or Europe.

Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco, dated to about 300,000 years ago, are the oldest known members of our species. Others come from Omo Kibish, Ethiopia (at least 233,000 years). The pattern suggests our species emerged across the continent, not in one “Garden of Eden.”
Older textbooks said about 200,000 years and pointed only to East Africa; new finds changed the picture, which is how science should work.
Hublin et al., Nature (2017); Vidal et al., Nature (2022)
Hublin et al. 2017, Nature: the Jebel Irhoud fossils

Engraved ochre from Blombos Cave in South Africa (about 75,000–100,000 years old) is among the earliest known symbolic marks. The Ishango bone from Congo (about 20,000 years old) carries grouped notches some scholars read as counting or arithmetic. Between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago groups of Africans spread out and populated the rest of the world.
How much the Ishango marks were “mathematics” is debated; that people in Africa were making symbols long before Europe is not.

Egypt unified around 3100 BCE and built one of history’s longest-lasting states. To its south, Nubian kingdoms (Kerma, then Kush) traded and fought with Egypt; Kushite kings ruled Egypt itself as its 25th Dynasty (8th–7th centuries BCE). Later, at Meroë, Kush smelted iron and built more pyramids than Egypt; Sudan has about 200 of them.

Aksum (in today’s Ethiopia and Eritrea) minted its own coins, traded across the Red Sea and Indian Ocean, and adopted Christianity in the 4th century under King Ezana, among the first states to do so. Islam arrived in Africa within the Prophet Muhammad’s lifetime, when early Muslims sheltered in Aksum, and spread across North and later West and East Africa.

West African empires grew rich from trans-Saharan trade in gold, salt and enslaved people. Mali’s ruler Mansa Musa made a pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 with so much gold that Arab writers said he depressed its value in Cairo. Timbuktu became a center of Islamic scholarship whose manuscripts survive by the hundreds of thousands. Songhai fell after a Moroccan invasion in 1591.

Great Zimbabwe’s stone city (11th–15th centuries) controlled gold trade to the Indian Ocean. Swahili city-states such as Kilwa traded with Arabia, India and China. The Kingdom of Kongo became Christian; in 1526 its king, Afonso I, wrote to Portugal’s king protesting that Portuguese traders were kidnapping his people.

White Rhodesian authorities insisted for decades that Africans could not have built Great Zimbabwe and pressured museums and guides to say otherwise, although archaeologists had shown in 1929 that it was African. An example of politics rewriting evidence.

For about twelve centuries captives from sub-Saharan Africa were taken across the Sahara, the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean to North Africa, the Middle East and Asia. Paul Lovejoy’s widely cited estimates total roughly 11 million (about 7.4 million across the Sahara and 3–4 million via the Red Sea and East Africa); others are lower. It is much less documented than the Atlantic trade.

About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto ships to the Americas; about 10.7 million survived the crossing. Most were bought from African rulers and merchants at coastal forts, not captured by Europeans directly. Kingdoms such as Dahomey and Asante grew powerful through the trade, while others, like Kongo’s Afonso I, protested it.

Western memory long focused on abolition, Africans as passive victims, or blamed “Africans selling Africans.” Each leaves out part: the trade was a partnership of European demand and capital with African elites, and its victims were ordinary Africans.
SlaveVoyages database (ship records for over 36,000 voyages)

Economist Nathan Nunn (2008) found that the parts of Africa that exported the most captives are the poorest today; a later study (Nunn and Wantchekon, 2011) found people in those areas report lower trust in neighbors and governments.
Nunn, Quarterly Journal of Economics (2008); Nunn and Wantchekon, American Economic Review (2011)

At the Berlin Conference (1884–85) European powers set rules for claiming African land; no African was present. By 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia were independent. Ethiopia defeated an Italian army at Adwa in 1896.

Imperial histories spoke of “civilizing missions” and ending the slave trade; African accounts emphasize conquest, resistance and land loss. Borders were drawn mostly by Europeans over decades of treaties, not at a single table in Berlin.

King Leopold II of Belgium ran the Congo Free State as his personal property. Forced rubber collection was enforced by hostage-taking, mutilation and killing. Missionaries, journalists and diplomats (Roger Casement’s 1904 report) exposed it, and Belgium took the colony over in 1908.
The number of deaths is debated: a figure of about 10 million is often cited, but census data from the time is poor. That mass killing and terror occurred is not in doubt.
Casement Report (1904); Hochschild, King Leopold’s Ghost (1998); demographers

German forces killed most of the Herero and about half the Nama in Namibia (1904–08); Germany acknowledged it as genocide in 2021. Britain detained tens of thousands of Kenyans in camps during the Mau Mau uprising (officially about 80,000; some historians argue far more) and paid £19.9 million to 5,228 victims in 2013. France fought a war to keep Algeria (1954–62) in which hundreds of thousands di

Some writers argue colonial rule also built schools, hospitals and railways (a 2017 article, “The Case for Colonialism”, was withdrawn after protests and threats). Critics answer that these served colonial needs and were paid for largely with Africans’ labor and taxes.
German government (2021); UK government (2013); historians

Ghana became independent in 1957; 17 countries followed in 1960, the “Year of Africa.” Portugal’s colonies won independence after long wars and a 1974 revolution in Lisbon. Zimbabwe (1980), Namibia (1990) and majority rule in South Africa (1994) completed the process.

Congo’s first elected prime minister, Patrice Lumumba, was killed in January 1961 with Belgian involvement (a Belgian inquiry in 2001 found “moral responsibility”); the CIA had separately plotted to poison him. The US then backed Mobutu’s dictatorship for three decades. In Angola, Cuba sent tens of thousands of troops against South Africa and US-backed rebels. South Africa secretly built six nucle
Belgian parliamentary inquiry (2001); Church Committee (1975); historians (Gleijeses)

Africa has seen over 200 coup attempts since 1950, about half successful. In the 1980s falling commodity prices and rising interest rates brought debt crises; the IMF and World Bank lent on condition of “structural adjustment”: cutting spending, selling state firms, opening trade.

In 1994 extremists killed an estimated 500,000 to about 1 million people (the UN and Rwanda’s government say about 1 million), mostly Tutsi, in about 100 days in Rwanda while the UN withdrew most peacekeepers. The aftermath spilled into Congo, where wars drew in eight African armies. An aid group estimated 5.4 million excess deaths there (1998–2007); other researchers argue that figure is much too
Colonial rulers had hardened Hutu and Tutsi into fixed racial categories on identity cards; a civil war and hate radio prepared the killing.
The Congo death toll is a classic statistics lesson: the estimate depends on what “normal” death rate you assume.
Established (genocide); Contested (Congo toll)
UN; International Rescue Committee; Human Security Report (2010)

Life expectancy in sub-Saharan Africa rose from about 50 in 2000 to over 60. Mobile money (Kenya’s M-Pesa, 2007) brought banking to millions. Botswana went from one of the poorest countries at independence (1966) to upper-middle income. The African Continental Free Trade Area began trading in 2021. Africa’s population is growing fastest in the world.
Western media often show Africa only through war and famine; boosters talk of “Africa rising.” Both are partial.

China became Africa’s largest trading partner and lent about $180 billion from 2000 to 2023 for roads, railways and ports. Russia’s Wagner group, later reorganized as the Africa Corps, provides security to several governments. Turkey, the Gulf states and India have grown too, while France’s influence has fallen sharply.
Western governments warn of Chinese “debt traps”; researchers such as Deborah Brautigam find little evidence that China seizes assets. African leaders often reply that they choose their own partners.

Military coups took Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger (2020–23). Their juntas expelled French and US forces, turned to Russia, formed the Alliance of Sahel States in September 2023 and left the West African bloc ECOWAS. They launched a joint force in December 2025 and expanded it in 2026; jihadist groups linked to al-Qaeda and the Islamic State still control large areas.
The deadliest jihadist insurgency in the world, poverty, and anger at France and at elected governments that failed to stop the killing.
The juntas present themselves as fighting for sovereignty against neo-colonialism; critics note elections cancelled, journalists jailed and civilian massacres by state forces and Russian mercenaries.

Sudan’s army and the Rapid Support Forces have fought since April 2023, creating the world’s largest displacement crisis; famine was declared in 2024 and mass killings were reported when the RSF took El Fasher in October 2025. In eastern Congo the M23 rebels, backed by Rwanda according to UN experts, took Goma in January 2025. Ethiopia’s Tigray war (2020–22) killed very large numbers; estimates va
Each side’s backers deny involvement; casualty counts are disputed because access is blocked.

Africa has deep histories told in archaeology, Arabic and Ge’ez manuscripts and oral tradition. Walter Rodney (How Europe Underdeveloped Africa, 1972) argued Europe’s wealth was built partly on Africa’s exploitation; Cheikh Anta Diop restored Africa’s place in ancient history.
Africa as a “dark continent” without history, needing civilization (Hegel in the 1830s; Trevor-Roper in 1963).
Institutions economists (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson; Nobel 2024)
Aid skeptics (Dambisa Moyo, Dead Aid, 2009)
African unity and self-reliance, “African solutions to African problems.”
The oldest Homo sapiens fossils and the greatest genetic diversity are African; every non-African population descends from Africans who left within the last ~70,000 years.
“Africans sold Africans,” so Europeans bear little responsibility.
Archaeology since 1929 shows it was built by the ancestors of the Shona; the outsider myth served white minority rule.
5.4 million people died in Congo’s wars.
An aid group’s estimate; other researchers using different baseline death rates find far fewer excess deaths. Statistics depend on assumptions.
UN World Population Prospects 2024 (approximate; * projection)
By 2050 about one person in four will be African.
The dip around 2000 reflects the HIV epidemic before treatment spread.

Each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs and squashes it. Training nudges every weight a tiny bit in the direction that reduces the error, over and over (gradient descent, with the nudges worked out by backpropagation). Nobody programs the rule “orange inside, blue outside”; the network finds it.

Try the spiral with 1 layer of 2 neurons: it can’t learn it. Add layers and neurons and it can. More capacity lets a model learn more complex patterns; too much, with too little data, and it memorizes noise instead (overfitting).

This network has a few dozen weights. GPT-3 (2020) had 175 billion, trained on hundreds of billions of words with the same basic recipe: predict, measure the error, adjust. Companies no longer publish sizes for most frontier models.

People reached the Americas from Asia at least 15,000 years ago, and footprints in New Mexico suggest earlier still. They built cities, empires, writing and mathematics entirely independently of the rest of the world.

After 1492 disease, conquest and enslavement remade the hemisphere: most Indigenous people died, millions of Africans were brought in chains, and Europeans built colonies that became today’s 35 countries.
About one third, with ≈8% of people (UNODC)

Human footprints at White Sands, New Mexico, dated to about 21,000–23,000 years ago, and the 14,500-year-old site of Monte Verde in Chile show people arrived earlier than the old “Clovis first” theory claimed. Genetics links Native Americans to ancient Siberian and East Asian populations.
Bennett et al., Science (2021); archaeology; genetics

The Olmec (from about 1200 BCE) carved colossal heads. The Maya built city-states, a full writing system and a base-20 number system with a symbol for zero, centuries before Europe adopted zero. Teotihuacan held perhaps 100,000 people. Lidar scans in 2024 revealed a network of 2,500-year-old cities in the Ecuadorian Amazon.
European conquerors burned most Maya books; only four survive. Modern decipherment (since the 1950s, with Russian linguist Yuri Knorozov’s key insight) recovered their voices.
Archaeology; Maya inscriptions; Rostain et al., Science (2024)

Tenochtitlan, the Mexica capital on a lake, had perhaps 200,000 people in 1519, larger than any city in Spain. The Inca ruled about 10 million people across the Andes, linked by some 40,000 km of roads, and kept records on knotted cords (quipu), an information system without writing.

Cahokia, near today’s St. Louis, was a city of perhaps 10,000–20,000 people around 1100. The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy united five, later six, nations under a Great Law of Peace. Hundreds of other nations lived across the continent.
Whether the Haudenosaunee influenced the US Constitution is debated; the US Congress acknowledged it in a 1988 resolution, while many historians think the influence was small.

After Columbus’s arrival in 1492, smallpox, measles and other diseases to which Native Americans had no immunity combined with war, enslavement and famine to kill perhaps 90% of the Indigenous population within about a century. Estimates of the pre-1492 population range from under 10 million to over 100 million; around 50–60 million is a common modern estimate.
The Americas had few domesticated animals, so few “crowd diseases” had developed there, while Europeans brought many.

The death toll is one of history’s most argued numbers because almost no counts exist. Some scientists even argue the regrowth of forests on abandoned farmland pulled enough carbon from the air to cool the world.
Demographic historians (Denevan, Cook); Koch et al. (2019)

Cortés took Tenochtitlan (1521) with a few hundred Spaniards and tens of thousands of Indigenous allies, above all the Tlaxcalans, after smallpox had struck the city. Pizarro captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa in 1532 as the empire emerged from a civil war. In 1550 the Spanish court held a formal debate (Valladolid) on whether the conquest was just, with Bartolomé de las Casas arguing for Indigen

The story of “a few hundred Spaniards” leaves out the Indigenous armies that did most of the fighting for their own reasons. Spain’s rivals later spread a “Black Legend” of Spanish cruelty to serve their own empires, which committed similar crimes.
Dependency theorists (Galeano’s Open Veins of Latin America, 1971) see the roots of underdevelopment here; others stress later policy choices. Galeano himself later said he would not reread the book.

About 10.7 million Africans survived the crossing to the Americas. Brazil received about 4.9 million, the most of any country; mainland North America received about 390,000 directly. Enslaved people resisted everywhere, forming free communities (quilombos, maroons) and revolts.

The US declared independence in 1776. In Haiti, enslaved people rose up in 1791 and founded the first Black republic in 1804. Simón Bolívar and José de San Martín led the wars that freed Spanish South America by 1825; Mexico became independent in 1821 and Brazil in 1822 as an empire.
Enlightenment ideas, Napoleon’s invasion of Spain (1808) and anger at colonial rule; in Haiti, the most brutal slave regime in the Americas.

In 1825 France forced Haiti to pay 150 million francs (later cut to 90 million) for its freedom under threat of invasion; a 2022 New York Times analysis estimated the long-run cost at $21–115 billion. The US refused to recognize Haiti until 1862.
Historians; French and Haitian records; New York Times (2022)

The 1823 Monroe Doctrine warned Europe away from the hemisphere. After Texas broke away (1836) and the US–Mexican War (1846–48), Mexico lost about half its territory. South America fought its own wars: Paraguay lost a large share of its population in the War of the Triple Alliance (1864–70) and Bolivia lost its coast to Chile (1879–84). Brazil abolished slavery last, in 1888.
Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848); historians

The US took Puerto Rico in 1898, helped Panama break from Colombia to build the canal (1903), and occupied Nicaragua (1912–33), Haiti (1915–34) and the Dominican Republic (1916–24), often to collect debts and protect US companies such as United Fruit.
A US Marine general, Smedley Butler, later wrote that he had been “a gangster for capitalism.” US officials at the time spoke of order and stability.

A revolution against the long dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz became a decade of civil war that caused over a million deaths (demographer Robert McCaa estimates about 1.4 million excess deaths). It produced a 1917 constitution with land reform and national ownership of oil, nationalized in 1938.
Mexico’s ruling party (PRI) made the revolution its founding story and then ruled for 71 years.

The CIA overthrew Guatemala’s elected government (1954); Cuba’s revolution (1959) aligned with the USSR; the US backed coups or military regimes in Brazil (1964), Chile (1973) and Argentina (1976), and the Contras in Nicaragua. Military regimes coordinated the killing of opponents across borders (Operation Condor). Leftist guerrillas also killed and kidnapped.

Supporters of the coups said they prevented communist dictatorships; victims’ families and truth commissions documented tens of thousands killed and disappeared. Some declassified US documents confirm detailed US knowledge.

When US interest rates soared, Mexico could not pay its debts (August 1982) and a crisis spread across the region: the 1980s became the “lost decade.” Governments then cut spending, sold state firms and opened trade, often as conditions of IMF and World Bank loans. NAFTA linked Mexico to the US and Canada in 1994; on the same day the Zapatista uprising began in Chiapas.
Debts taken on in the 1970s at low rates, oil shocks, inflation and US monetary policy.
Free-market economists point to Chile’s growth and falling poverty; critics point to inequality, crises (Argentina 2001) and the backlash that followed.

Left-wing governments won elections in Venezuela (Chávez, 1999), Brazil (Lula, 2003), Bolivia (Morales, 2006) and elsewhere. High commodity prices funded social programs; poverty fell sharply across the region.
Disappointment with the 1990s reforms and rising demand from China for oil, soy and metals.
Venezuela’s collapse and the 2026 US raid (developing)

Under Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela’s economy collapsed, with hyperinflation and shortages; about 8 million people emigrated. Elections were widely judged unfair. On 3 January 2026 US forces struck Caracas and captured Maduro and his wife, flying them to New York to face narco-terrorism charges; Venezuela’s top court made Vice-President Delcy Rodríguez interim president.
Oil dependence, price collapse after 2014, mismanagement, corruption and US sanctions after 2017.

Mexico’s drug war has seen over 450,000 homicides since 2006 and over 100,000 people missing. Colombia signed peace with the FARC guerrillas in 2016. El Salvador’s Nayib Bukele jailed tens of thousands of suspected gang members under a state of emergency since 2022; murders fell dramatically while rights groups documented abuses. Gangs control much of Haiti’s capital.

China became South America’s largest trading partner and opened a mega-port at Chancay, Peru in 2024. Canada, a parliamentary federation since 1867, has reckoned with the residential schools that took about 150,000 Indigenous children from their families (Truth and Reconciliation Commission, 2015).
Inequality and the social costs of the 1990s reforms.
Spain brought language, faith, universities and laws; the “Black Legend” exaggerated its crimes.
The Americas were mostly empty wilderness in 1492.
Most Indigenous deaths after 1492 came from deliberate killing.
Disease killed most, but war, enslavement and famine made epidemics far deadlier, and some killing was deliberate.
Brazil received about 4.9 million; mainland North America about 390,000 directly.
France demanded 150 million francs in 1825 under threat of war; Haiti paid for decades.
Congress said so in 1988; many historians find little direct evidence.
The 2026 US capture of Maduro was legal under international law.
How many people lived in the Americas in 1492? Different scholars’ estimates (millions)
SlaveVoyages: records of over 36,000 slaving voyages

The constitution (rewritten again in March 2026 to drop reunification, add a territory clause and name Kim head of state) makes the State Affairs Commission, chaired by Kim Jong Un, the top state body. The Supreme People’s Assembly is the legislature; the Cabinet under a Premier runs the economy. The party’s rules rank above the constitution in practice.

Three legal parties: the Workers’ Party of Korea (WPK) leads; the Korean Social Democratic Party and the Chondoist Chongu Party sit inside a front it controls and never run against it. Leninist “democratic centralism”: decisions flow down, dissent is forbidden once a line is set.
One approved candidate per district; turnout reported near 100%. Voting is a loyalty check, not a choice.

Formally state-owned and planned. In practice, private markets (jangmadang) that grew after the 1990s famine feed most families; rich traders (donju) finance housing and businesses under official cover. Sanctions cut most legal trade.
Foreign currency flows to the leadership through party-run trading firms, arms sales, workers abroad and cyber theft; since 2024 weapons and troops for Russia.
An army of over a million soldiers, nuclear weapons and missiles. The Ministry of State Security runs political prison camps; a UN inquiry (2014) estimated 80,000–120,000 prisoners.

Family ties (Kim Yo Jong), the Organization and Guidance Department that vets every official, and personal loyalty decide careers. Purges and executions of top officials (Jang Song Thaek, 2013) show the stakes.
General Secretary, head of state, supreme commander; leader since 2011.
The innermost circle; re-elected at the Ninth Congress (2026).
How North Korea abandoned reunification (2023–2026)
At a party plenum in December 2023 Kim said the two Koreas were now two hostile states.
In January 2024 he told the Supreme People’s Assembly to rewrite the constitution and called the South the “principal enemy.”
The Ninth Party Congress (February 2026) reaffirmed the line and re-elected Kim.
Soviet occupation; Kim Il Sung installed; the state founded in 1948.
Kim Il Sung dies; famine; Kim Jong Il’s military-first rule.
Party congresses revived; 2024 “two hostile states”; alliance with Russia.
It has survived famine, sanctions and two hereditary successions; experts disagree on how markets, smuggled media and a young population change that.
Neither 30 years of sanctions nor periods of engagement stopped the nuclear program; scholars disagree about why.
A one-party communist state running a market economy. Power was shared among four top leaders for decades; in 2026 the party chief also became head of state.

The 2013 constitution names the Communist Party “the force leading the State and society.” The National Assembly elects the President, Prime Minister and Assembly Chair, and passes laws; courts and prosecutors answer to the party.

One legal party. The National Party Congress (every five years) elects a Central Committee (200 in 2026), which elects the Politburo (19) and General Secretary. Unlike North Korea, the Central Committee really votes and has overruled leaders (2016).
State firms dominate energy, banking and telecoms; private firms and foreign investors (Samsung, Intel, Apple suppliers) drive exports. The 1986 Đổi Mới reforms opened the economy.
Influence works through party networks, provincial leaders and state-business ties; the anti-corruption “blazing furnace” campaign removed presidents, ministers and tycoons since 2016.
In 2025 the 63 provinces were merged into 34 and the district tier abolished. Provincial party secretaries are stepping stones to the Politburo.
No independent courts or press. Checks come from inside the party: Central Committee votes, the Inspection Commission, and collective leadership norms, which the 2026 merger of top posts weakened.
General Secretary (2024) and State President (2026).
Le Minh Hung since 2026; runs the economy.
How a leadership contest was decided inside the party (2016)
The Central Committee’s vote on the candidate list before the 12th Congress (January 2016) went against Dung.
Anti-corruption purges; two presidents resign (2023, 2024).
A presidential democracy since 1987 with a strong single-term president, two big parties, powerful family conglomerates (chaebol), and courts and protests that have removed two presidents.
A president elected directly for one five-year term; a 300-seat National Assembly; a Constitutional Court that can remove an impeached president.
Turnout around 75–80% in presidential elections. 254 single-member districts plus 46 proportional seats (since 2024); regional voting patterns (southwest vs southeast) remain strong.
Strong courts, a free press and mass protest. In December 2024 lawmakers overturned martial law within hours; the president was removed in 2025 and sentenced to life in 2026.
Elected June 2025 after his predecessor’s removal.
Used for martial law in 2024; refused to go further.
Organized the 2016–17 candlelight protests.
How democracy survived martial law (2024–2026)
On 3 December 2024 President Yoon declared martial law and sent troops to the National Assembly.
Within about two and a half hours, 190 lawmakers who got inside voted unanimously to lift it; Yoon withdrew it before dawn.
The Assembly impeached him on 14 December; the Constitutional Court removed him unanimously on 4 April 2025.
Lee Jae-myung won the June 2025 election.
In February 2026 a court found Yoon guilty of leading an insurrection and sentenced him to life in prison.
Military rule (Park Chung-hee, Chun Doo-hwan); Gwangju 1980.
Every president since 1987 has ended in scandal or prosecution, including family members; many propose constitutional change.
Today (developing, with its evolution since 1979)

A theocratic republic: elected presidents and parliaments operate inside a system controlled by an unelected Supreme Leader, clerical councils that vet candidates, and the Revolutionary Guards. In 2026 a US–Israeli war killed the Supreme Leader, and his son succeeded him.

The 1979 constitution (revised 1989) gives final authority to the Supreme Leader under velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the Islamic jurist). The president runs the government; the Majlis passes laws; the Guardian Council can veto them.
Regular elections, but the 12-member Guardian Council vets every candidate: in 2024 it approved 6 of 80 presidential hopefuls. Turnout has fallen sharply as many boycott.
Two armies: the regular army and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), which also commands the Basij militia and regional allies. The Guards’ influence grew sharply during the 2026 war.

Courts serve the system; protest movements (2009, 2019, 2022 “Woman, Life, Freedom”, and the 2025–26 nationwide uprising, in which thousands were killed) were crushed. Elections offer limited choice among approved candidates.
Chosen in March 2026 after his father was killed.
How a Supreme Leader was chosen in wartime (2026)
Ali Khamenei was killed in a US–Israeli strike on 28 February 2026.
The 88-member Assembly of Experts met in Qom; some members said they were not informed of the session.
On 9 March it named his son Mojtaba Khamenei, reportedly under pressure from the Revolutionary Guards.
Critics call it hereditary succession, which the 1979 revolution condemned; supporters call it continuity in wartime.
Green Movement, fuel protests, “Woman, Life, Freedom.”
A president elected in two rounds for four years (one re-election allowed consecutively), a Congress of 513 deputies and 81 senators, and a Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF) with wide powers.
About twenty parties hold seats. Presidents build “coalitional presidentialism”: they trade ministries and budget amendments for votes, especially with the flexible center bloc (“Centrão”).
Voting is compulsory from 18 to 70; electronic voting delivers results within hours. In October 2026 Lula won a fourth term with about 52% after losing the first round.
Congress members control billions in budget amendments (emendas) for their bases. Corporate donations to campaigns were banned in 2015; public campaign funds replaced them.
The military ruled 1964–85 and kept influence; officers were among those convicted over the 2022 coup plot.
A federation of 26 states and the federal district; governors are major power brokers.
Caucuses cut across parties: agribusiness (“ruralistas”), evangelicals, security forces (“bullet caucus”).
Re-elected October 2026 for a fourth term.
Ruled 1964–85; officers convicted in 2025.
How Brazil judged a coup plot (2022–2026)
Jair Bolsonaro lost the 2022 election to Lula and did not clearly concede.
On 8 January 2023 his supporters stormed Congress, the presidential palace and the Supreme Court.
In September 2025 a Supreme Court panel convicted him and sentenced him to 27 years.
In 2026 his son Flávio ran, lost the runoff narrowly and refused to recognize the result.
A federal presidential democracy, ruled by one party for 71 years until 2000, now dominated again by a new party, Morena, which holds a supermajority and in 2024 made judges elected.
A president elected for one six-year term (no re-election ever), a Congress, and since the 2024 reform a judiciary chosen by popular vote.
Morena (founded 2014 by Andrés Manuel López Obrador) dominates; the old PRI and the conservative PAN are weakened.
Competitive elections run by an independent electoral institute (INE). The first judicial election (June 2025) drew about 13% turnout.
TV networks (Televisa, TV Azteca) and social media; journalists are frequently killed, mostly in regions where cartels and local officials collude.
32 states with governors; local politics often entangled with organized crime.
Cartels, which fund campaigns and kill candidates in some regions; the US government, through trade and security pressure.
An electoral institute, a free but endangered press. Critics argue the 2024 judicial reform and dissolution of independent regulators weakened checks.
Since October 2024; first woman president.
Morena and allies won a supermajority in June 2024.
Despite strikes by court workers and protests, the reform passed in September 2024.
In June 2025 voters chose thousands of judges; about 13% turned out.
López Obrador; Morena dominance; Sheinbaum elected 2024.

A parliamentary democracy since 1994 with one of the world’s strongest constitutions. The ANC, which led the fight against apartheid, ruled alone for 30 years until 2024, when it lost its majority and formed a coalition.

Willem Einthoven recorded the first practical electrocardiogram in 1903 (Nobel 1924). The P wave is the atria contracting, the QRS spike is the ventricles firing, and the T wave is them resetting. The first time your immune system meets a pathogen, building antibodies takes 1–2 weeks. Memory B and T cells then remain, so a second exposure triggers a faster, larger response that often stops illness. Vaccines provide the first exposure safely. Edward Jenner’s smallpox vaccine (1796) began the field; smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.

A beam’s resistance to bending depends on its second moment of area, I, which grows with the cube of depth and rewards putting material far from the center (the neutral axis). A PID controller adjusts output from the error now (Proportional), the accumulated past error (Integral) and how fast the error is changing (Derivative). Gear ratio = teeth on driven gear ÷ teeth on driver. A bigger driven gear turns slower but with more torque (turning force); power stays the same minus friction. The Antikythera mechanism (Greece, around 100 BC) used about 30 bronze gears to predict eclipses.

Sample a wave too slowly and you get a fake wave. It’s why wagon wheels spin backward in films.

The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem (Nyquist 1928, Shannon 1949): to capture a frequency you must sample more than twice as fast. Below that, a high frequency masquerades as a lower one (aliasing). CDs sample at 44,100 Hz to capture sounds up to about 20,000 Hz, the upper limit of human hearing.
Digital audio, phone cameras, medical imaging, radar, the “wagon-wheel effect” in film and moiré patterns on screens.

Start at 2 and cross out every multiple of it, then move to the next number that is still standing and cross out its multiples. Whatever survives can’t be divided by anything smaller, so it is prime. You only need to sieve up to √400 = 20.

Primes are the atoms of arithmetic. They keep your bank and messages secure (RSA encryption), they pick hash table sizes in software, and cicadas emerge on prime-year cycles (13 and 17) which may help them avoid predators.

Caesar shifted letters by 3; it falls to frequency analysis, invented by al-Kindi in the 800s, because E is the most common English letter. RSA (1977) uses two large primes: anyone can encrypt with the public key (n, e), but decrypting needs d, which requires knowing n’s prime factors. Multiplying primes is easy; factoring their product is very hard.

RSA and its successors protect online banking, HTTPS, messaging apps and digital signatures. Codebreaking at Bletchley Park shortened World War II. Quantum computers could one day break RSA, which is why “post-quantum” cryptography is being rolled out.

Only five solids have identical regular faces with the same number meeting at every corner; Euclid proved there can be no others. For any such solid, vertices − edges + faces = 2 (Euler, 1758), the first result of topology.
Viruses form icosahedral shells; methane is a tetrahedron; crystals and dice use these shapes; Buckminster Fuller’s domes and the C₆₀ “buckyball” molecule are cousins.
A Voronoi diagram splits space by nearest point. John Snow used the idea in 1854 to show cholera deaths clustered around one London water pump, a founding moment of epidemiology.

Galileo noticed (around 1602, watching a cathedral lamp) that a pendulum’s period barely depends on how far it swings. The period is T ≈ 2π√(L/g): only length and gravity matter, not mass. Huygens built the first pendulum clock in 1656, improving timekeeping roughly 60-fold.
Clocks for 270 years, measuring gravity for oil prospecting, Foucault’s pendulum proving Earth rotates (1851), seismometers, and the physics of any oscillation.

Waves superpose: their heights add. Thomas Young’s double-slit experiment (1801) used this pattern to prove light is a wave. The bright and dark bands depend on wavelength and source spacing.
Noise-cancelling headphones, concert hall acoustics, phased-array radar and 5G beamforming, gravitational-wave detectors (LIGO), and holograms.

Protons set the element (its atomic number); neutrons make isotopes; electrons set the charge and chemistry. Electrons fill shells (2, 8, 8, 18…); the outer shell decides how an atom bonds. Rutherford found the nucleus in 1911; Bohr proposed shells in 1913.
All of chemistry, nuclear power and medicine (isotopes), carbon dating, semiconductors (silicon with 4 outer electrons) and understanding why noble gases don’t react.

pH = −log₁₀ of the hydrogen ion concentration (Søren Sørensen, 1909, at the Carlsberg brewery). pH 7 is neutral; each unit down is 10× more acidic. Because it is logarithmic, pH 3 is 10,000× more acidic than pH 7.

When a planet passes in front of its star, brightness drops by (planet radius ÷ star radius)². Jupiter dims the Sun about 1%; Earth only about 0.008%. NASA’s Kepler and TESS missions found thousands of planets this way, using statistics to pull tiny dips out of noise.
Over 5,000 exoplanets confirmed (NASA, 2022 onward), searching for Earth-like worlds and reading their atmospheres with JWST.

All recorded history fits in the last ~35 seconds of the year.

The Moon is always half lit by the Sun; phases are how much of that lit half we see from Earth. A full cycle takes about 29.5 days. Eclipses need a new or full Moon exactly in line, but the Moon’s orbit is tilted about 5°, so most months miss.

A polarizer passes light whose waves vibrate along its axis. Étienne-Louis Malus found in 1809 that the fraction passing is cos²θ, where θ is the angle between filters. For single photons this fraction becomes a probability: each photon either passes or not, and passing resets its polarization to the new filter’s angle. So a 45° filter between two crossed ones turns “impossible” into a 25% chance.
Sunglasses, LCD screens, 3D cinema glasses, and quantum cryptography (the BB84 protocol, 1984), whose security rests on measurement disturbing photons.

You start with $50,000. Pick how many households to insure and what to charge. Survive 20 years without going bankrupt, and don’t overcharge so much that customers leave.

Modern insurance grew out of Edward Lloyd’s coffee house in London around 1688, where merchants met to share the risk of ships being lost at sea. Today insurers spread disaster risk further by buying insurance themselves (reinsurance) and by selling “catastrophe bonds”. Hurricane Andrew in 1992 bankrupted several Florida insurers. It was a correlated disaster of exactly the kind the checkbox adds.

Energy is lost at each step up a food chain. A cow uses most of the plant energy it eats to live, move and keep warm, so only a few percent becomes meat. That is why animal foods, especially beef and lamb, need far more land than plants for the same protein. Poore and Nemecek (2018) combined about 38,700 farms in 119 countries to measure this.
Your city has a million people who each need about 50 g of protein a day. Design a menu that keeps them fed on less than 2,000 km² of farmland. What do you have to give up, and what do you keep?

To answer the second question you must compare explanations: how likely is the evidence under each one?

In 1947 Judge Learned Hand said an owner’s duty depends on three things: the probability (P) that an accident happens, the size of the loss (L) if it does, and the burden (B) of taking precautions. A minister asks: “Which economy is bigger, the US or China?” The honest answer is “for what?”. Pick the right measure for each real decision.

The IMF projects that in 2026 the US stays ahead at market exchange rates by about $11 trillion, while China stays ahead at PPP by about $12 trillion, and the PPP gap is growing. Both statements are true at once. Which one a politician or newspaper quotes often tells you which argument they are making.

In the simple supply-and-demand model, a ceiling below the market price creates a shortage (more people want it than is supplied); a floor above it creates a surplus. Real markets can differ: with employer market power (monopsony), a moderate minimum wage can raise both pay and jobs (Card & Krueger, 1994), a point economists still debate.

Textbook competitive model. Debates: supporters of rent control cite stability for tenants; most economists cite reduced supply and quality (e.g. Diamond, McQuade & Qian on San Francisco, 2019). Minimum wage studies range from small job losses to none at moderate levels.

David Ricardo (1817): what matters is comparative advantage, the opportunity cost of each good. If Portugal is better at both but relatively better at wine, both countries end up with more by specializing and trading. Gains are real for countries overall, but some workers and regions lose (e.g. the “China shock” to US manufacturing towns, Autor, Dorn & Hanson, 2013).

You and 4 computer fishers share a lake. Overfish and it collapses. Can rules save it?

Garrett Hardin (1968) argued shared resources get overused because each user gains from taking more while costs are shared. Elinor Ostrom (Nobel 2009) showed many communities avoid this with local rules, monitoring and sanctions, not only through private property or government control.
Fisheries (the Grand Banks cod collapse of 1992), groundwater, climate change, antibiotics, traffic congestion and open-source software.

Banks keep a fraction of deposits as cash and lend the rest. That creates money and credit, but means the bank can’t pay everyone at once. Diamond and Dybvig (1983, Nobel 2022) showed runs can be self-fulfilling: if you think others will withdraw, withdrawing is rational. Deposit insurance (FDIC, 1933) and central banks as lenders of last resort exist to stop this.
The Great Depression (about 9,000 US banks failed 1930–33), Northern Rock (2007), Silicon Valley Bank (2023, $42 billion withdrawn in one day), and stablecoins today.
Government spends $100. The worker spends some, the shopkeeper spends some… how big does it get?

Keynes (1936) argued spending ripples through the economy: if people spend a fraction c of each extra dollar, total demand rises by 1/(1−c) times the original. Leakages (saving, taxes, imports) shrink it, and if the economy is at full capacity or the central bank raises rates, crowding out can cancel much of it. Estimates of real multipliers range from about 0.5 to 2.
Stimulus debates (2009, 2020–21), austerity in Europe after 2010, tax cuts versus spending, and how local economies respond to a new factory or base.

The Marquis de Condorcet (1785) found majority preferences can cycle even when every individual is consistent. Kenneth Arrow (1951) proved no ranked voting system can satisfy a short list of fairness conditions at once. So the rules for counting votes can change the winner.
A real-style parliament with no majority. Find coalitions that reach 50% + 1, then count how much power each party really has.

J. Ridley Stroop (1935) found people are slower to name ink colors when the word names a different color. Reading is so automatic it interferes with the task. It is a classic measure of attention and self-control.

In the Müller-Lyer illusion (1889) a line with outward fins looks longer than an identical line with inward fins. One theory: our visual system reads the fins as corners of rooms, as near or far edges. Studies across cultures (Segall, Campbell & Herskovits, 1966) found the effect varies, possibly with exposure to rectangular buildings, though this is debated.

Tversky and Kahneman’s “Asian disease problem” (1981): when options were framed as lives saved, 72% chose the sure option; framed as deaths, 78% chose the gamble, though the outcomes were identical. Losses loom about twice as large as equal gains (prospect theory; Kahneman’s 2002 Nobel).
Medical decisions (90% survival vs 10% mortality), political messaging, marketing, insurance, investing (holding losers too long), and public health communication.

B. F. Skinner (1930s–50s) found behavior rewarded unpredictably (variable-ratio schedules) is learned persistently and is hardest to extinguish. Fixed schedules create pauses after each reward. Pavlov (1890s) showed the related classical conditioning with dogs and bells.

Ernst Weber (1834) and Gustav Fechner (1860) found the just-noticeable difference is a constant fraction of the stimulus (about 2–3% for weights, roughly 8–10% for areas). So perception works on ratios, like a logarithm: going from 1 to 2 candles feels like 10 to 20.
Why decibels and the Richter scale are logarithmic, pricing ($9.99 vs $10), sound engineering, and the psychology of money (an extra $100 matters less to a rich person).

Thomas Schelling (1971) used coins on a checkerboard: agents move if fewer than a threshold share of neighbors are like them. Even a 33% preference produces highly segregated patterns. It shows macro outcomes don’t require extreme individual attitudes. It is not a full explanation of real segregation, which was also driven by laws and policies like redlining and restrictive covenants.

Stanley Milgram’s 1967 letter-passing experiment suggested about six steps link strangers in the US. Watts and Strogatz (1998) showed why: a few random shortcuts in a mostly local network dramatically shrink average distances while keeping friend groups clustered. Facebook measured an average of about 3.6 degrees between its users in 2016.
How diseases, rumors and job information spread (Granovetter’s “strength of weak ties”, 1973), network design, epidemics and influencer marketing.

Mark Granovetter (1978): each person has a threshold, the number of others who must act before they join. With thresholds 0, 1, 2, … 99, one instigator triggers everyone. Change a single person from 1 to 2 and nothing happens. The same crowd with almost the same attitudes can produce a revolution or nothing.
Why revolutions surprise experts (1989 in Eastern Europe, the 2011 Arab Spring), fashion and technology adoption, bank runs and viral content.

Mobility matrices give the chance a child ends up in each income fifth given their parents’. Raj Chetty’s team (2014) found a US child born in the bottom fifth has about a 7.5% chance of reaching the top fifth, varying from about 4% to 13% by region. Over generations, low mobility locks in advantage.

Capitalism is an economic system in which most land, factories, machines and businesses are privately owned, people work for wages, prices are set mostly by buying and selling in markets, and owners invest in order to make a profit. Markets and money are thousands of years old; capitalism as a whole system grew up in Europe from about the 1500s and took off with the Industrial Revolution in Britai

It is the system most people alive today live under, in very different forms: the United States, Sweden, Japan, Singapore, Chile and India are all capitalist, yet their taxes, welfare states, unions and state ownership differ hugely. So the useful question is rarely “capitalism, yes or no?” but “which version, for whom, with what results?”

Its record includes the largest rise in living standards in human history and some of its worst crimes. Since 1820 the share of humanity in extreme poverty has fallen from the large majority to about one in ten, and life expectancy has more than doubled. Splitting work into many small specialized tasks makes each worker far more productive. Adam Smith’s pin factory: ten workers each doing one step made about 48,000 pins a day; one person alone might make twenty.

Smith himself warned that endless repetition could make workers “stupid and ignorant” and urged public education; Marx called it alienating.

When people trade freely, each seeking their own gain, prices guide resources to where they are most wanted, without anyone planning it. Smith used the phrase “invisible hand” only once in The Wealth of Nations.
David Ricardo (1817) showed that two countries both gain from trade even if one is better at making everything, as long as each specializes in what it is relatively best at.

In 1958 Mao launched the Great Leap Forward to overtake Britain’s industry within 15 years. Farmers were put into giant communes, pulled off the fields to make steel in backyard furnaces, and told to use untested methods. Local officials, afraid of being purged, reported harvests far larger than real ones.

The state took grain according to those false figures, so villages were left with too little. Grain was still exported to pay debts. When the defence minister Peng Dehuai criticised the policy at the Lushan meeting in 1959, he was purged and the campaign intensified. In Xinyang prefecture alone, about one person in eight died.
The policy was reversed in 1961–62. For decades the official name was “three years of natural disasters”; drought and floods did happen, but economists find they explain only part of the deaths.

In World War II, Allied spies and aerial photos suggested Germany was building over 1,000 tanks a month. Statisticians took a different route: captured tanks carried sequential serial numbers on their parts. If you capture k tanks and the highest number you see is m, the best estimate of the total is m + m/k − 1.

For June 1940 the statistical estimate was 169 tanks against an intelligence estimate of 1,000; German records later showed 122. For June 1941: 244 (statistics), 1,550 (intelligence), 271 (actual). For August 1942: 327, 1,550 and 342. Spies and photos, influenced by fear, overestimated by about five times; arithmetic did not.
Ruggles and Brodie, Journal of the American Statistical Association (1947)

In 1943 the US Statistical Research Group studied bullet holes in returning bombers. The obvious answer was to armor the most-hit areas. The mathematician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: these were the planes that survived. Planes hit in the engines mostly did not return, so the missing holes showed where armor was needed.
Wald (1943, reprinted 1980); Mangel and Samaniego, JASA (1984)
How sure is “probably”? Bayes and intelligence failures

In 1964 CIA analyst Sherman Kent found that colleagues reading “serious possibility” in a report understood it as anything from about 20% to 80% likely. In 2002 a US intelligence estimate judged with “high confidence” that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction; none were found. Reviews blamed treating evidence that fit the expected answer as stronger than it was. Bayes’ rule says how much each piec

In a US intelligence research tournament (2011–15), teams of trained volunteers who thought in explicit probabilities, the “superforecasters” studied by Philip Tetlock, reportedly outperformed professional analysts.

Thomas Schelling (Nobel 2005) applied it to nuclear deterrence. An arms race is a prisoner’s dilemma: each side arms because the other might, and both end up poorer and less safe. In many real datasets (populations, prices, accounts) about 30% of numbers start with 1 and fewer than 5% with 9. People who invent numbers spread first digits too evenly. Auditors and courts use this as a red flag.

A 2011 study of EU economic data found Greece’s figures deviated most from Benford’s law in the years before its debt crisis, when its deficit statistics were later shown to have been misreported. Benford is a flag, not proof: honest data can fail it and clever fraud can pass, and it works poorly for vote counts.

At 7% growth an economy doubles every 10 years; at 2% every 35. South Korea grew around 7% or more for decades; many countries grew 1–2%. The same math works on debt: Latin American governments borrowed in the 1970s at low, floating rates; when US rates jumped toward 20% around 1981, payments exploded and Mexico could not pay in 1982.
The “lost decade” that followed cut incomes across Latin America. Haiti’s 1825 indemnity to France, repaid with interest over decades, is a similar story of compounding.
Use the rule of 70: doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ growth rate. It explains wealth gaps, debt crises and savings.

If each infected person infects R others, cases grow exponentially when R is above 1. In the Americas after 1492 nobody was immune to smallpox or measles, so R was high and deaths were catastrophic. In 1854 John Snow mapped cholera deaths around a London water pump and showed the disease spread through water, founding epidemiology.
Herd immunity starts when a share 1 − 1/R of people are immune: about 80% for R = 5, over 90% for measles. Vaccination ended smallpox in 1980, the first disease eradicated.
How do we know humans are 300,000 years old?

Radioactive atoms decay at fixed rates. Carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years) dates organic remains up to about 50,000 years. Potassium–argon and argon–argon dating of volcanic ash reaches millions of years. Thermoluminescence measures when flint was last heated. Genetics adds a “molecular clock” from mutation rates.

These independent methods date the Jebel Irhoud fossils in Morocco to about 300,000 years and place the main human spread out of Africa around 50,000–70,000 years ago. Radiocarbon also dated the Shroud of Turin to 1260–1390 CE (1988), a result some believers still dispute.
Hublin et al., Nature (2017); Damon et al., Nature (1989)

About 500 related Bantu languages are spoken across central, eastern and southern Africa, while their closest relatives cluster near today’s Nigeria–Cameroon border. Linguists concluded Bantu speakers spread out from there. Archaeologists found pottery and iron-working spreading the same way over the last 3,000–5,000 years. Geneticists then found the matching DNA trail.
Three independent kinds of evidence (words, objects, genes) tell the same story. Today over 350 million people speak Bantu languages, including Swahili, Zulu and Kikongo.
Linguistic, archaeological and genetic studies (e.g., Patin et al., Science, 2017)

In 1977 psychologists Hasher, Goldstein and Toppino found that people rate statements as more likely true simply because they have heard them before: the illusory truth effect. It works even when people know better. Propaganda ministries in every era relied on repetition.
Hasher, Goldstein and Toppino (1977); later replications

The 1815 eruption of Tambora in Indonesia threw so much ash into the stratosphere that 1816 became the “year without a summer”: crops failed in Europe and North America, and famine and typhus followed. Ice cores, tree rings and cave deposits now let scientists date droughts and cold spells across centuries.

Historians link climate shocks to crises such as the 17th-century wave of wars and revolts and droughts during the collapse of some Classic Maya cities, though how much climate caused versus how societies responded remains debated.
Ice-core and tree-ring studies; Parker, Global Crisis (2013)

Fission was discovered in 1938. Natural uranium is about 0.7% uranium-235; power reactors use 3–5%; weapons use about 90%. Because enrichment gets easier at each step, a country at 60% is most of the way to weapons-grade.

That physics shapes treaties and crises from Iran’s enrichment to North Korea’s bombs. South Africa built six nuclear weapons and dismantled them around 1990, the only country to give up weapons it built itself.
Understanding the physics shows which claims about “peaceful programs” are plausible.

In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically, so famine must follow. In the 1960s experts again predicted mass famine. Instead, high-yield wheat and rice bred by Norman Borlaug and others, plus fertilizer and irrigation, tripled harvests in much of Asia.

World food per person rose even as population doubled. Famines since 1950 have mostly come from war and politics (China 1959–61, Ethiopia 1984, North Korea in the 1990s), not from absolute shortage, as economist Amartya Sen showed.

The Mercator projection (1569) preserves angles for navigation, so it stretches areas near the poles. Greenland looks as big as Africa, which is actually about 14 times larger. Africa (about 30 million km²) could hold the US, China, India and most of Europe.

After World War II the Dutch painter Han van Meegeren was arrested for selling a “Vermeer”, a national treasure, to Nazi leader Hermann Göring. To escape a treason charge he confessed he had painted it himself, and painted another “Vermeer” to prove it.

The intelligence (“Ultra”) helped win the Battle of the Atlantic. Official historian Harry Hinsley estimated it shortened the war by about two years, an estimate others debate. The work fed directly into early computers.

Two ideas hold the field together. Every living thing is made of cells, and every living thing descends from common ancestors through evolution. As the geneticist Theodosius Dobzhansky put it in a famous 1973 essay, nothing in biology makes sense except in the light of evolution. DNA is the chemical record of that shared history: humans share genes with yeast, flies and bananas.

Biology has doubled human life expectancy. Germ theory, vaccines, antibiotics, insulin and higher-yielding crops came from it. It has also been misused. “Race science” and eugenics led to forced sterilization and fed the Nazi genocide; the Tuskegee study withheld treatment from Black men for decades; Soviet politics crushed genetics. New tools such as gene editing raise hard questions again.
Almost every trait comes from genes and environment working together. Beware anyone who says “it’s all genes” or “genes don’t matter”.

All living things are made of one or more cells, and every cell comes from another cell. Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann proposed cell theory in 1838–39; Rudolf Virchow added in 1855 that all cells come from cells.
Your body has roughly 30 trillion human cells and a similar number of bacterial cells.

Individuals vary; some variations help survival and reproduction; those are passed on, so populations change over generations. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace announced the theory in 1858; Darwin’s On the Origin of Species followed in 1859.
Bacteria evolve resistance to antibiotics within years; Darwin’s finches’ beaks change after droughts (the Grants’ 40-year study).
Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859), Project Gutenberg
Traits are passed on in discrete units, now called genes. Gregor Mendel showed this with peas in 1856–63 (published 1866); his work was ignored until 1900.
Genes are made of DNA. Its double-helix structure, solved in 1953 by James Watson and Francis Crick using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, showed how it copies itself.
Confirmed by every experiment since; the full human genome was published in 2003, with the last gaps filled in 2022.
Only about 1–2% of human DNA codes for proteins; what much of the rest does is still debated.
DNA is copied into RNA, which is translated into proteins, using a three-letter code shared by almost all life. Francis Crick stated the “central dogma” in 1958; the code was cracked in the 1960s.
Many diseases are caused by microorganisms. Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch proved it in the 1860s–1880s; Koch identified the bacteria behind anthrax (1876), tuberculosis (1882) and cholera (1883).

Living bodies keep internal conditions (temperature, blood sugar, salt) within narrow limits using feedback. Claude Bernard described the internal environment in the 1850s–70s; Walter Cannon named homeostasis in 1926.
Insulin lowers blood sugar after a meal; in type 1 diabetes the body cannot make it.

Living things and their surroundings form ecosystems (Arthur Tansley named them in 1935). Energy flows from the Sun through plants to animals, and only about 10% passes up each level of the food chain.
Measured in field studies worldwide; the 10% figure is a rough average.
The oxygen in the air was produced by photosynthesis, starting with cyanobacteria over 2 billion years ago.
It is inefficient (about 1–2% of sunlight becomes plant mass in most crops); researchers try to improve it.
Vaccines train immune memory without the disease; smallpox was eradicated by 1980.
Nobel Prize 1995 (genetic control of development)

The nervous system is built from separate cells, neurons (Santiago Ramón y Cajal, 1880s–90s), which send electrical signals. Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley explained the nerve impulse mathematically in 1952.
Leeuwenhoek’s lenses (1670s), electron microscopes, cryo-EM (Nobel 2017)
Goodall’s chimpanzees (from 1960), the Grants’ finches (from 1973)

On the Beagle voyage (1831–36) Charles Darwin collected evidence that species change. He worked on the theory privately for 20 years until Alfred Russel Wallace independently reached the same idea in 1858. Their joint papers were read that year, and On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859.
Misused as “social Darwinism” to justify inequality and racism, which Darwin’s science does not support.

Gregor Mendel, a monk in Brno, crossed about 28,000 pea plants and found that traits are inherited as separate units in predictable ratios (such as 3:1). His 1866 paper was ignored until three scientists rediscovered it in 1900.

In 1847 Ignaz Semmelweis cut deaths from childbed fever in his Vienna ward by making doctors wash hands in chlorinated lime, but colleagues rejected him. Louis Pasteur showed microbes cause fermentation and spoilage and developed vaccines; Robert Koch identified the microbes behind anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera.
Semmelweis’s handwashing cuts maternal deaths sharply.
Semmelweis was ignored and died in an asylum in 1865.

Francis Galton coined “eugenics” in 1883, the idea of improving humanity by controlling who reproduces. It became mainstream in many countries. The US Supreme Court upheld forced sterilization in Buck v. Bell (1927), and over 60,000 Americans were sterilized. Nazi Germany sterilized about 400,000 people and moved on to murder disabled people.
Embryo screening raises debates some call “new eugenics”; others say voluntary choices are different.

Oswald Avery’s team showed in 1944 that DNA carries genes. In 1953 Watson and Crick built the double-helix model, using X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin and Raymond Gosling (including Photo 51) that Maurice Wilkins showed them without Franklin’s knowledge. Franklin died in 1958; the 1962 Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins.
Franklin’s data and analysis were essential; recent research suggests she was more a collaborator than a victim of theft.

Trofim Lysenko, a Soviet agronomist, rejected genetics and claimed crops could be changed by their environment. Backed by Stalin, he had genetics banned. The great plant geneticist Nikolai Vavilov was arrested and died in prison in 1943. Soviet genetics was set back a generation.

Scientists imprisoned or killed; failed farm methods; China adopted some Lysenkoist practices during the Great Leap Forward, whose famine killed tens of millions (how much the methods contributed is debated).

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that a mould killed bacteria. Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley turned it into a drug in 1940–41, and US companies mass-produced it during the war. In his 1945 Nobel lecture Fleming warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria. He was right.
Antimicrobial resistance directly causes about 1.27 million deaths.

Chemistry is the science of what things are made of and how they change into other things. Everything you can touch is built from about 90 naturally occurring elements, combined into millions of compounds. Chemistry explains why iron rusts, how bread rises, why medicines work and how a battery stores energy.

For most of history people knew a great deal of practical chemistry (metalwork, dyes, soap, brewing, glass) without knowing why it worked. Alchemists searched for ways to turn lead into gold. Modern chemistry began when people started weighing things carefully: in the 1780s Antoine Lavoisier showed that matter is conserved in reactions, and by 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev had arranged the elements into t

Chemistry may have changed daily life more than any other science. Synthetic fertilizer helps feed about half of humanity. Antibiotics, plastics, clean drinking water and lithium batteries are all chemistry. So are chemical weapons, leaded petrol, the Bhopal disaster, the hole in the ozone layer and “forever chemicals” in drinking water. The same knowledge produced all of them.

In a chemical reaction atoms are rearranged, never created or destroyed, so the total mass stays the same. Antoine Lavoisier showed this in the 1770s–80s by weighing everything, including gases, in sealed containers.

An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. John Dalton proposed in 1808 that each element has atoms of a characteristic weight, and that compounds form from fixed whole-number ratios of atoms.
Established; atoms were made directly visible by scanning tunnelling microscopes in the 1980s.
Arranging elements by atomic weight (later atomic number) makes their properties repeat in a pattern. Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869 left gaps for unknown elements and predicted their properties.
His “eka-aluminium” was found as gallium in 1875, with almost exactly the density he predicted.

Atoms stick together by sharing electrons (covalent bonds), transferring them (ionic bonds) or pooling them (metallic bonds). Gilbert Lewis (1916) and Linus Pauling (1930s) explained bonds with electron pairs and quantum mechanics.
Atoms are too small to count, so chemists count them by mass. One mole is 6.02214076 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro’s number, fixed exactly since 2019).
18 grams of water is one mole: about 600 billion trillion molecules.
Many reactions run both ways until forward and backward rates balance. If you change conditions, the balance shifts to oppose the change (Henri Le Chatelier, 1884).
Acids give up hydrogen ions; bases take them. The pH scale (Søren Sørensen, 1909) measures acidity: each step is a factor of ten.
Lemon juice is about pH 2, blood about 7.4; the oceans have become about 30% more acidic since the industrial era as they absorb CO₂.
Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2018 (directed evolution of enzymes)

Carbon forms four bonds and long chains and rings, making millions of compounds. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a compound from living things, from non-living chemicals, weakening the belief that life’s chemicals needed a “vital force”.
Long chains of repeating units. Hermann Staudinger argued in the 1920s that these “macromolecules” were real, against fierce opposition (Nobel Prize 1953). Wallace Carothers made nylon in 1935.
Reactions that move electrons can make electricity (batteries) or be driven by it (electrolysis). Alessandro Volta built the first battery in 1800.
The lithium-ion battery (Nobel Prize 2019: Goodenough, Whittingham, Yoshino) powers phones and electric cars.
Established; lithium-ion costs fell about 97% between 1991 and 2018 (Ziegler and Trancik, 2021).
Merging with biology and computing (AlphaFold, Nobel 2024).
Design processes that avoid hazardous substances and waste (12 principles, Anastas and Warner, 1998).
Yields fall at each step; a 20-step synthesis can lose most of the material. Scaling to a factory raises new problems.
Woodward’s synthesis of vitamin B12, modern drug routes
Bunsen and Kirchhoff discovered caesium and rubidium this way (1860–61); NMR and infrared reveal molecular structure.
Used in drug tests, food safety and forensics; Mikhail Tsvet separated plant pigments this way in the 1900s.
Rosalind Franklin’s Photo 51 was key evidence for DNA’s double helix; Dorothy Hodgkin solved penicillin, vitamin B12 and insulin.
Nobel Prizes 1998, 2013 and 2024 (protein structure prediction)
US TSCA (1976, revised 2016), EU REACH (2007), Chemical Weapons Convention (1997)
Many older chemicals were grandfathered in with little testing; testing has improved since the 2000s
Only about 9% of plastic waste was recycled worldwide in 2019 (OECD)

Chemists believed burning released a substance called phlogiston. Antoine Lavoisier, weighing everything in sealed vessels, showed that burning combines a substance with a gas he named oxygen. He set out conservation of mass and a modern naming system. During the French Revolution he was guillotined in 1794 for his role as a tax collector.
Joseph Priestley isolates “dephlogisticated air” (oxygen); Carl Scheele had found it independently.

Several chemists noticed patterns among elements. Dmitri Mendeleev’s 1869 table was the boldest: he left gaps and predicted three missing elements and their properties. Gallium (1875), scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) were found as predicted.
John Newlands’s “law of octaves” is ridiculed.
Elements up to 118 have been made; all spaces in the first seven rows are filled.

After Henri Becquerel found that uranium emits invisible rays, Marie Curie measured them, named the effect radioactivity and, with Pierre Curie, discovered polonium and radium (1898). She is the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences (physics 1903, chemistry 1911).
Dies of aplastic anaemia, likely from radiation.

Fritz Haber found how to make ammonia from nitrogen in the air (1909), and Carl Bosch scaled it up (1913). Synthetic fertilizer from the Haber–Bosch process now helps feed roughly half the world’s people. Haber also led Germany’s chemical weapons programme and oversaw the first large chlorine gas attack at Ypres in 1915.
His wife, the chemist Clara Immerwahr, dies by suicide; her reasons are debated.
Forced out by Nazi laws because he was Jewish; dies in exile in 1934.
Chemical weapons; gas killed about 90,000–100,000 soldiers in the First World War.
Nitrogen run-off causes dead zones in rivers and seas and adds greenhouse gases.
About 1–2% of world energy goes into making ammonia; greener methods are being researched.

In 1921 Thomas Midgley at General Motors found that tetraethyl lead stops engines knocking. Despite worker deaths at plants in the 1920s, it was sold worldwide for decades. Geochemist Clair Patterson showed that lead pollution was everywhere, against fierce industry opposition. The last country stopped selling leaded petrol for cars in 2021.
Lead lowers children’s IQ and is linked to heart disease; a 2022 study (McFarland and others, PNAS) estimated leaded-petrol exposure cost Americans alive in 2015 about 824 million IQ points in total.
The early worker deaths and Patterson’s data.
A case of profit and doubt delaying action for 50 years.
Lead from old paint and pipes remains a hazard (Flint, Michigan, 2014).

Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), invented in 1928 as safe refrigerants, seemed perfect. In 1974 Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland predicted they would destroy stratospheric ozone, which shields life from ultraviolet light. In 1985 British scientists found an ozone hole over Antarctica. The 1987 Montreal Protocol phased CFCs out, and the ozone layer is recovering.
UN assessment: on track to recover by about 2066 over Antarctica.
Some replacements (HFCs) are powerful greenhouse gases, now being phased down under the 2016 Kigali Amendment.
Illegal CFC emissions detected from China in 2018 fell after enforcement.

Paul Müller found DDT’s insect-killing power in 1939 (Nobel Prize 1948). It helped stop typhus and malaria and was sprayed on farms worldwide. Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring (1962) documented harm to wildlife, especially birds. The US banned most uses in 1972; the 2001 Stockholm Convention allows it only for disease control.
Malaria still kills about 600,000 people a year (WHO); DDT is one tool among bed nets and medicines.

Thalidomide was sold from 1957 as a sedative and morning-sickness remedy. It caused severe birth defects in more than 10,000 children worldwide. Frances Kelsey of the US Food and Drug Administration refused to approve it, and the disaster led to modern drug-testing laws.
More than 10,000 children harmed; many died.

On the night of 2–3 December 1984, about 40 tonnes of methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a Union Carbide pesticide plant in Bhopal, India. Thousands died within days, and hundreds of thousands were injured. It remains the deadliest industrial disaster in history.
Union Carbide pays $470 million settlement.
Official immediate death toll about 3,800; other estimates exceed 15,000 over time; long-term illness and contaminated groundwater.

Stanley Whittingham made a lithium battery in the 1970s; John Goodenough found a better cathode (1980); Akira Yoshino made a safe, workable design (1985); Sony sold the first commercial cells in 1991. Costs fell so far that electric cars and grid storage became practical.
Erisman et al., Nature Geoscience (2008)
Chlorination helped cut typhoid deaths dramatically in the 20th century
Synthetic drugs, from aspirin (1899) to modern antivirals
Lithium-ion cost down about 97% (1991–2018)
Plastics production about 460 million tonnes (2019)
About 90,000–100,000 deaths; over a million casualties
Banned by the 1925 Geneva Protocol and the 1997 Chemical Weapons Convention.
About 3,800 immediate deaths; estimates over 15,000 over time
About 22 million tonnes leaked into the environment (2019)
Health effects for some PFAS established; Developing regulation.
Wöhler made urea in 1828; all of life’s molecules can now be made.
Gallium, scandium and germanium exist (Mendeleev, 1869–71)
Burning coal will warm the Earth (Arrhenius, 1896)
CFCs will destroy ozone (Molina and Rowland, 1974)
Megadoses of vitamin C prevent colds and cancer (Pauling, 1970s)
How strictly should “forever chemicals” (PFAS) be regulated?
US drinking-water limits set in 2024 are being revised; deadlines may change.
The OPCW verified destruction of all declared stockpiles by 2023.
Syria used sarin and chlorine; Novichok poisonings in 2018 and 2020.
Pencil “lead” is graphite (carbon) and clay.
Large studies found no link; thimerosal was removed from US childhood vaccines by 2001 anyway.
Faraday, The Chemical History of a Candle (1861), Project Gutenberg
Le Couteur and Burreson, Napoleon’s Buttons (2003)
Roberts and Tren, The Excellent Powder (2010), against the DDT ban
Oreskes and Conway, Merchants of Doubt (2010)
