10 landmark cases: heroes, disasters and fixes

Mathematics began with practical needs: counting herds, measuring fields after the Nile flooded, taxing harvests and predicting the seasons. Babylonian scribes were solving quadratic problems on clay tablets around 1800 BCE. The Greeks then made the leap that defines the subject: they demanded proof, so that a statement is accepted only when it follows by logic from simpler ones.
Babylonian tablet Plimpton 322 lists Pythagorean triples, over 1,000 years before Pythagoras.
Euclid’s Elements organizes geometry as proofs from five postulates. It was used as a textbook for over 2,000 years.
Andrew Wiles completes the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, open for 357 years.
Founded algebra as a subject; his name gives us “algorithm.”
Plimpton 322, a Babylonian clay tablet of number pairs (c. 1800 BCE).
The Rhind Papyrus: Egyptian math problems copied around 1550 BCE.
A papyrus fragment of Euclid’s Elements found at Oxyrhynchus, Egypt, copied about 1,900 years ago.
Al-Khwarizmi’s book on algebra (c. 820).
Newton’s Principia (1687), where calculus-style reasoning explains the heavens.
How do computers “think” with 1s and 0s?
Chrysippus and the Stoics develop logic of “if… then” statements.
George Boole publishes The Laws of Thought: logic as algebra with 1 and 0.
Founded modern logic with quantifiers (“for all,” “there exists”).
Principia Mathematica (1910–13): hundreds of pages before proving 1 + 1 = 2.
Writing “if X then Y” rules precisely is how you write code and testable hypotheses.

People built calculating aids for millennia (the abacus, Pascal’s adding machine), but computer science began with a question in logic: is there a mechanical method to decide any mathematical statement? Alan Turing answered “no” in 1936 by imagining a universal machine, and that imaginary machine became the blueprint for every computer. World War II codebreaking and ballistics turned the idea into
The Dartmouth workshop names the field “artificial intelligence.”
Kept neural networks alive through decades of doubt; Nobel Prize in Physics 2024.
Babbage’s Analytical Engine, designed in the 1830s and never finished.
ENIAC (1945) filled a room and used about 18,000 vacuum tubes.
Others argue they manipulate statistical patterns without grounding, goals or experience, so “understanding” is the wrong word.

Probability began at the gambling table. In 1654 a gambler asked Blaise Pascal how to split the pot of an unfinished game fairly, and Pascal’s letters with Pierre de Fermat founded the theory. Statistics grew from the needs of states (the word comes from “state”) to count people, trade and deaths, and then from science’s need to separate real effects from noise.
How can a sample of 1,000 people describe 300 million?
What does “statistically significant” really mean?
John Graunt analyzes London’s death records: the first demography.
Bayes’s essay on updating beliefs with evidence is published after his death.
John Snow maps cholera deaths around a London water pump.
Used statistical charts to prove that bad sanitation killed more soldiers than battle.
Gave probability its rigorous axioms (1933).
Championed exploring data visually; coined the word “bit.”
John Snow, who traced London’s 1854 cholera outbreak to a single water pump by mapping where the victims lived.
A backtest is a statistical claim: ask how many strategies were tried before this one “worked.”
Critics (including the American Statistical Association in 2016) say it is widely misread and encourages chasing significance; they favor effect sizes, intervals and Bayesian methods.
Galileo’s Sidereus Nuncius (1610): the first telescope discoveries.
Trinity, the first nuclear explosion, July 1945.
Estimating with powers of ten (“Fermi problems”) is a skill for any decision.
Lavoisier states conservation of mass and lists 33 elements.
Founded modern chemistry; executed in the French Revolution.
Photo 51 (1952), the X-ray image of DNA taken in Rosalind Franklin’s lab.
Robert Hooke sees “cells” in cork through a microscope.
Alexander Fleming notices penicillin killing bacteria.
Hooke’s Micrographia (1665), the first book of microscope drawings.

Farmers needed to predict seasons and floods; sailors needed stars and currents; miners needed to know where ore lies. Earth science also changed how we see time itself: rocks showed that Earth is billions of years old, not thousands.
How do we know what the climate was 100,000 years ago?
James Hutton argues Earth’s rocks record “no vestige of a beginning.”
The Blue Marble, Earth photographed by Apollo 17 (1972).
Earthrise, taken by Apollo 8 astronaut Bill Anders (1968).
Pale Blue Dot: Earth from 6 billion km away, Voyager 1 (1990).
The Hubble Ultra-Deep Field: about 10,000 galaxies in a tiny patch of sky.
Pangaea, the supercontinent of about 300–200 million years ago.

Merchants, kings and philosophers always argued about prices, money and taxes, but economics became a field in the 1700s when thinkers asked why some nations were getting richer. Adam Smith’s answer, the division of labor and trade guided by self-interest within rules, started a debate that still decides elections.
Why did the world get so much richer after 1800?
The Wealth of Nations; the “invisible hand.”
First edition of The Wealth of Nations (1776).
The Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, where 44 Allied nations designed the postwar money system in 1944.
Crowds on Wall Street after the 1929 crash.

Whenever people live together they must decide who decides. Political thought began with questions about justice and the best constitution in Greece, China and India; political science grew as a field in the 1800s and 1900s as democracies spread and scholars began measuring elections, wars and institutions.
Without a state, life is “nasty, brutish, and short.”

Rulers always thought about rivers, mountains and trade routes. As a named field, geopolitics arose around 1900 when strategists like Alfred Thayer Mahan (sea power) and Halford Mackinder (the “heartland”) tried to explain why some empires rose. It was later tainted by Nazi use, then revived to explain the Cold War and today’s US–China rivalry.
Mackinder’s “The Geographical Pivot of History.”
Münster’s town hall, where part of the Peace of Westphalia (1648) was signed.
Europe’s borders as redrawn by the Congress of Vienna (1815).
Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin at Yalta, February 1945.
Are the US and China headed for war (the “Thucydides Trap”)?
Graham Allison found that in 12 of 16 historical cases of a rising power challenging a ruling one, the result was war.

Philosophers argued about the mind for millennia. Psychology became a science in 1879 when Wilhelm Wundt opened the first laboratory to measure mental processes. It has since swung between studying inner experience, observable behavior and the brain itself.
A large project replicates only about 36–39% of 100 psychology studies.
Phineas Gage survived an iron rod through his skull in 1848; his personality changed.
Auguste Comte coins the word “sociology.”
Race, “double consciousness,” early data sociology.
Hull House, Chicago, a settlement house founded in 1889.
Jacob Riis, whose photographs in How the Other Half Lives (1890) exposed New York’s tenements.

European contact with peoples worldwide raised a question: are human differences biological or cultural? Anthropology took shape in the 1800s, often entangled with colonialism and racist theories, and was remade in the 1900s by fieldworkers like Franz Boas and Bronisław Malinowski, who lived with the people they studied and argued that cultures must be understood on their own terms.
The fossil “Lucy” (Australopithecus afarensis), about 3.2 million years old, found in Ethiopia.
Excavations begin at Göbekli Tepe, monuments roughly 11,000 years old.
Sequenced the Neanderthal genome; Nobel 2022.
Lascaux cave paintings, about 17,000 years old.
The Venus of Willendorf, about 30,000 years old.
Long human history puts recent “unprecedented” claims in perspective.
Emblem of the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg (1945–46).
History from archives, “as it actually was.”
The Rosetta Stone (196 BCE): the key to Egyptian hieroglyphs.
The Bayeux Tapestry: the Norman conquest of England, 1066.
A detail of the Catalan Atlas (1375), among the finest maps of its age.

Philosophy began when people stopped accepting myths as explanations and asked for reasons. Around the same era (roughly 800–200 BCE), Greece, India and China each produced thinkers (Socrates, the Buddha, Confucius, Laozi) who asked how to live and what is real. Most sciences started as branches of philosophy.
Descartes’ Meditations: “I think, therefore I am.”
Raphael’s The School of Athens (1509–1511): Plato and Aristotle at the center.
Jacques-Louis David’s The Death of Socrates (1787).
How do religions answer suffering and death?
Luther’s 95 Theses begin the Protestant Reformation.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, the oldest known Hebrew Bible manuscripts.
The Diamond Sutra (868 CE), the oldest dated printed book.

Ancient grammarians, especially Pāṇini in India (around the 4th century BCE), described languages with stunning precision to preserve sacred texts. In 1786 William Jones noticed that Sanskrit, Greek and Latin share a common ancestor, launching historical linguistics; in the 1950s Noam Chomsky argued that humans share an inborn capacity for grammar.
Chinese oracle bones, about 3,000 years old.
How do novels change politics (Uncle Tom’s Cabin, 1984)?

Art is older than writing: cave paintings and bone flutes date back more than 35,000 years. Art served religion, power and memory, then became a field of study in its own right in the Renaissance, when artists were also scientists of perspective, anatomy and light.
Hokusai’s The Great Wave off Kanagawa (c. 1831).

Healing is as old as humanity, but for most of history doctors could do little and often did harm. Medicine became effective in the last 200 years through anatomy, germ theory, anesthesia, vaccines, antibiotics and the controlled trial, which finally let doctors find out what works.
Why did life expectancy roughly double after 1900?
Made mRNA vaccines possible; Nobel 2023.

Engineering is as old as cities: aqueducts, roads, bridges and siege machines. It became a profession with the steam engine and railways in the 1700s and 1800s, and engineering decides how much energy, food and information each person can command.
The first powered flight, 17 December 1903.
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse, 1940.
The Tuskegee study (1932–1972), a turning point in research ethics.
Newton’s laws are not “wrong”: they are extremely accurate for everyday speeds and sizes and fail near light speed or at atomic scales. Learn where each theory works.
A measurement without an error bar is not a result. Many famous “discoveries” vanished when the uncertainty was checked.

Objects keep moving in a straight line unless a force acts on them; force equals mass times acceleration; every action has an equal and opposite reaction. The same gravity that makes an apple fall keeps the Moon in orbit. Isaac Newton published this in the Principia in 1687.
Newton, Principia (1687), English translation on Wikisource
Confirmed to great accuracy at everyday speeds; in 1846 it predicted the planet Neptune before anyone saw it. It breaks down near light speed (relativity) and at atomic scales (quantum).

Energy is never created or destroyed, only converted: chemical to heat, heat to motion, motion to electricity. James Joule’s experiments in the 1840s showed that a fixed amount of work always makes the same amount of heat.

No confirmed violation has ever been found. In 1930 Wolfgang Pauli trusted it so much that he predicted an invisible particle, the neutrino, to balance the books in radioactive decay; it was detected in 1956.

In an isolated system, disorder (entropy) tends to increase. Heat flows from hot to cold, never the reverse on its own. This is the second law of thermodynamics, and it is why no engine can be 100% efficient.
Never violated in a large system. Ludwig Boltzmann explained it statistically: there are vastly more disordered arrangements than ordered ones.

Electricity and magnetism are two faces of one force. In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote four equations describing it and found they predict waves travelling at the speed of light: light itself is an electromagnetic wave.
Maxwell, A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field (1865)
Heinrich Hertz made and detected radio waves in 1887–88, confirming Maxwell. The quantum version (quantum electrodynamics) is among the most precisely tested theories in science.
The equations assumed a medium (the “aether”) for light to travel in; experiments found no aether, which led to relativity.

In 1905 Albert Einstein showed that the speed of light is the same for everyone, so time and space must stretch: moving clocks run slow and nothing with mass can reach light speed. Mass and energy are equivalent (E = mc²).
Einstein, Relativity: The Special and General Theory (1916), Project Gutenberg
Confirmed by atomic clocks flown on planes (Hafele–Keating, 1971), particle lifetimes and every particle accelerator.

Einstein’s 1915 theory says mass and energy curve space and time, and objects follow the curves. It predicted that light bends around the Sun, that clocks run slower in strong gravity, black holes, and ripples in spacetime called gravitational waves.
GPS satellites’ clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast compared with the ground; without relativity corrections, positions would drift by kilometres a day.
LIGO, the first detection of gravitational waves (2016)
Every test has passed: the 1919 eclipse, Mercury’s orbit, gravitational waves (2015) and the first image of a black hole’s shadow (2019).

At atomic scales, energy comes in packets (quanta), particles behave like waves, and results are probabilities: you can predict exactly how often an outcome happens, but not which one happens next. Built by Planck, Einstein, Bohr, Heisenberg, Schrödinger, Dirac and others between 1900 and 1930.
The most successful theory ever built: some predictions match experiment to better than one part in a billion. Bell-test experiments (Nobel Prize 2022) confirmed its strangest feature, entanglement.
Physicists still disagree about what it means: whether the wave is real, whether measurement “collapses” it, or whether all outcomes happen (see Debates).

Everything is made of atoms; each atom is a tiny, heavy nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons around it. Protons and neutrons are made of quarks. The Standard Model lists 17 kinds of fundamental particle, and the Higgs boson was the last one found (2012).
Established. The 1909–11 gold-foil experiment revealed the nucleus; particle accelerators confirmed every predicted particle of the Standard Model.
Attempts at a “theory of everything” (string theory, loop quantum gravity) remain untested.

Waves carry energy without carrying matter. They reflect, bend, spread and interfere. Thomas Young’s double-slit experiment (about 1801) showed light makes interference patterns, so it behaves as a wave.

In 1929 Edwin Hubble, building on measurements by Vesto Slipher and theory by Georges Lemaître, showed distant galaxies are moving away from us, faster the farther they are. Running the film backwards gives the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago.
The cosmic microwave background, the afterglow of the early universe, was found by accident in 1965 by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson.
About 95% of the universe’s content is dark matter and dark energy, which no one has identified.

Physics runs on measurement. Since 2019 every SI unit, including the kilogram, has been defined by fixing the value of a fundamental constant, such as Planck’s constant, instead of by a metal object in a vault.
Every result in physics is a number with an uncertainty; discoveries in particle physics require “5 sigma”, roughly a one-in-3.5-million chance of a fluke.
The 5-sigma rule doesn’t protect against systematic errors, such as a loose cable (see the OPERA case).
Standard Model complete since 2012; dark matter not explained.
Galileo 1609, Hubble Space Telescope 1990, James Webb 2021, the Event Horizon Telescope
Enormous cost and international politics; CERN’s Large Hadron Collider is a 27 km ring built by dozens of countries.
LIGO’s 4 km arms detect changes in length far smaller than a proton, so it must filter out trucks, earthquakes and ocean waves.
Units used to rely on physical objects that drifted; since 2019 they rest on fixed constants of nature.
Scientific ignition reached at NIF in 2022, but no fusion power plant yet
How to read a measurement’s uncertainty, and what “5 sigma” means.

Galileo Galilei argued, against Aristotle, that heavy and light objects fall at the same rate if air resistance is ignored, and he measured motion with rolling balls on ramps. In 1609–10 he turned an improved telescope on the sky and saw Jupiter’s moons and the phases of Venus, evidence for Copernicus’s Sun-centred system.
Telescope observations; publishes Sidereus Nuncius (1610).
Galileo is a symbol in every argument about science and authority. See the lab “Religion and science: the real history”.

Isaac Newton showed that one law of gravity explains both falling objects and the orbits of the Moon and planets. His Principia (1687) set out three laws of motion and universal gravitation and became the model for all later physics.

Physicists thought light must travel through an invisible “aether”, so Earth’s motion through it should change light’s measured speed in different directions. Albert Michelson and Edward Morley built an interferometer sensitive enough to detect it, and found no effect. This “null result” helped lead to relativity.
Modern versions test the constancy of light speed to parts in 10^17.
That the 1919 data alone were not decisive; later, better tests were.
Light bending is now measured with radio telescopes to better than 0.1%.

In 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann split uranium; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it as nuclear fission. Fearing Nazi Germany would build a bomb, scientists alerted the US government. The Manhattan Project employed over 100,000 people and built the bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.
Hiroshima and Nagasaki: about 150,000–246,000 deaths within two to four months (RERF estimates).
A nuclear arms race; about 12,000 warheads still exist.
The bombs forced Japan’s surrender and avoided an invasion that would have killed even more people.
Deliberately targeting cities killed civilians on a vast scale and was unnecessary or immoral.
The scale of expected casualties from an invasion and Japan’s leaders’ resistance to surrender.

In March 1989 chemists Martin Fleischmann and Stanley Pons announced at a press conference that they had produced nuclear fusion at room temperature in a tabletop cell. Labs worldwide tried to repeat it within weeks. Most found nothing, and the claim was rejected.
That no reliable, replicable result has appeared in over 30 years.

The OPERA experiment timed neutrinos sent from CERN to Gran Sasso in Italy and found them arriving about 60 nanoseconds too early, faster than light. The team asked others to find their error. In 2012 it was traced to a badly connected fibre-optic cable and a clock problem.
A large collaboration with careful statistics (6 sigma) but a hidden systematic error.

In 1964 Peter Higgs, François Englert, Robert Brout and others proposed a field that gives particles mass, which predicts a new particle. After decades of searching, the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider announced its discovery on 4 July 2012.
ATLAS and CMS announce a new particle at about 125 GeV.

Einstein predicted ripples in spacetime in 1916 but thought they would be too weak ever to detect. On 14 September 2015 the two LIGO detectors in the United States recorded the signal of two black holes merging about 1.3 billion years ago.
A binary pulsar indirectly confirms them (Nobel 1993).
About 91% of the world’s people had access by 2022
From one transistor (1947) to tens of billions on a chip
Needs relativity corrections of about 38 microseconds a day.
Cost of solar electricity fell about 85–90% in the 2010s
The photoelectric effect (Einstein, 1905) underlies it.
About 150,000–246,000 deaths within 2–4 months
31 short-term deaths; WHO estimated up to 4,000 eventual cancer deaths among the most exposed

The earthquake and tsunami left about 18,000 dead or missing.
Federation of American Scientists (2025)

Physics knowledge is neutral; its uses are not. These costs come from weapons, accidents and early ignorance of radiation. Per unit of electricity, nuclear power’s death rate is among the lowest of any energy source (Our World in Data), which shows why context matters.
A new planet beyond Uranus (Le Verrier and Adams, 1846)
A planet “Vulcan” inside Mercury’s orbit (Le Verrier, 1859)
Proton decay (grand unified theories, 1970s)
Not seen; protons live longer than 10^34 years if they decay at all.
Fusion power plants within decades (since the 1950s)
Ignition achieved in 2022; no power plant yet.
Two precise methods give different expansion rates (about 67 vs 73 km/s/Mpc), suggesting something missing.
Try the lab “Measure how fast the universe is expanding”.
Smolin, Woit, Hossenfelder: after 50 years it makes no testable predictions; beauty is not evidence.
CERN’s proposed Future Circular Collider (about 91 km) would study the Higgs in detail and search for new physics.
Very low carbon emissions and among the lowest deaths per unit of energy.
Compare deaths and emissions per terawatt-hour (Our World in Data).
Without air resistance, all objects fall at the same rate; Apollo 15’s David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon in 1971.
At the ISS’s height gravity is about 90% as strong as on the ground; astronauts float because they are falling around Earth.
A “measurement” in quantum mechanics doesn’t need a conscious observer; this is a misreading.

The USSR grew fast from 1928 to the 1970s, then stalled and collapsed in the 1990s. China was among the poorest countries on earth until 1978, then grew faster than any large economy in history.
Same language, culture and history until 1945. By 2018 the South was more than 20 times richer per person by these estimates.

It looks like a clean natural experiment, but not everything else was equal: the South got large US aid and markets, the North got Soviet aid until 1991, and the North started with more industry. North Korea publishes almost no data, so its numbers are rough outside estimates.
Around 1700 the gap between northwest Europe and China or India was modest. By 1900 Britain was several times richer per person.
Around 1900 Argentina was among the richest countries per person. Venezuela was the richest in South America in the 1950s–70s; then it collapsed.
Oil made some states rich fast, but income swings with oil prices. Iran stagnated after 1979.

Measured as the share of people who can’t afford a basic bundle of food, shelter and other needs where they live (the “cost of basic needs” method). Critics such as Jason Hickel argue poverty lines are set too low and that early estimates miss subsistence living outside markets; defenders like Max Roser and Michail Moatsos reply that the decline holds across most reasonable lines.
Moatsos (2021), OECD “How Was Life? Vol. II”, via Our World in Data.
Early figures come from signatures on marriage records and census questions, so they are rough. The broad rise from about 1 in 8 to more than 8 in 10 is well documented.
OECD and UNESCO (2019) via Our World in Data.

In 1914 Britain ruled the largest empire in history. By the early 1920s it covered about a quarter of the world’s land and over 450 million people, and London was the centre of world finance. Fifty years later the empire was almost gone, and the United States led the world’s money system, its biggest military alliance and hundreds of military bases on every continent.

The handover was not a single event. It happened through two world wars that bankrupted Britain and enriched America, loans with conditions attached, a new money system designed at Bretton Woods in 1944, the independence of India and dozens of other colonies, and moments of open humiliation such as the Suez Crisis of 1956. It was also a partnership: the “special relationship”, shared intelligence
Both empires brought trade, law and institutions, and both killed and impoverished millions. The tables show both.

Control of the oceans lets a power protect its trade and move armies. Britain aimed from 1889 for a navy as large as the next two combined (the “two-power standard”); the US Navy became the world’s strongest after 1945.
Naval historians such as Alfred Thayer Mahan (1890) argued sea power decides the fate of great powers; evidence is strong but not absolute.
The currency other countries hold as savings and use for trade gives its issuer cheap borrowing and influence. The pound sterling held this role before 1914; the US dollar took it after 1945.
About 58% of the world’s official foreign-exchange reserves were in dollars in 2024 (IMF).

The Bretton Woods conference (1944) pegged currencies to the dollar and the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce.
Institutions still exist; the gold link ended in 1971.
Between 1945 and 1975 most colonies won independence. Britain’s empire shrank from hundreds of millions of subjects to a few small territories.

Fascism was a form of politics born in Europe after the First World War. It combined extreme nationalism, the cult of a single leader, one mass party with its own uniformed squads, the destruction of elections, free unions and opposing parties, and violence presented as cleansing the nation and giving it a rebirth. Nazism (National Socialism) was the German form, led by Adolf Hitler. What set it apart was biological racism and antisemitism at its very core. It led to the Holocaust: the murder of about six million Jews, along with Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Polish and Soviet civilians and many others. Scholars genuinely debate many questions. What counts as fascism? Was it of the left or the right? How was the Holocaust decided? Why did millions support it? And how far can the word be stretched today? This deep dive shows each school at its strongest. It also covers the people who resisted and rescued, the countries that collaborated, the trials afterward, and how each country remembers.

A note for readers: this topic includes genocide and mass murder. Descriptions are factual and not graphic, and no images of the dead are shown. The site does not label any present-day party or politician fascist. Where scholars, courts or governments have used the word, both their view and the response of those they describe are given.
Whether the Holocaust happened is not a debate. How it was decided, why people took part, and how to define fascism are real debates among historians.
Fascist regimes used soft words for terrible things: “Final Solution”, “euthanasia”, “pacification”. The Words section explains each one.

The nation, imagined as one living body, comes before the individual, before social class and before any rights. Mussolini put it in a 1925 speech roughly as “everything within the state, nothing outside the state”, and the philosopher Giovanni Gentile built a theory around it.
Italian schoolchildren swore loyalty to the Duce; German civil servants and soldiers swore an oath to Hitler personally from August 1934.
The Doctrine of Fascism (1932), Britannica summary
In practice the “nation” meant the regime: critics, minorities and anyone outside the approved community lost their rights.
After a world war that killed millions, many people longed for unity, pride and belonging above party squabbles.

Fascists said the nation had become weak and decadent and must be reborn through a revolutionary new order. The historian Roger Griffin calls this the core myth of fascism: “palingenetic ultranationalism”, meaning nationalism built on the myth of rebirth.
Nazi propaganda spoke of a “national awakening” in 1933; Mussolini promised a new Roman empire.
Influential among historians as a definition (see Debates); critics say it fits many movements that never acted like fascist regimes.

All authority flows down from one leader, and all loyalty flows up. Germans called it the Führerprinzip; Italians chanted “Il Duce ha sempre ragione” (the Duce is always right). Führer, Duce, Caudillo, Poglavnik and Conducător all mean “leader”.
The historian Ian Kershaw found that officials competed to “work towards the Führer”, guessing what Hitler wanted and acting before being told.
Kershaw, Working Towards the Führer (1993)

Fascists praised action over talk and saw violence as healthy and cleansing. They despised parliament and debate as weak. Both movements had uniformed squads: Italy’s Blackshirts (squadristi) and Germany’s Brownshirts (SA).
In 1920–22 Fascist squads burned hundreds of socialist offices and union halls in northern Italy; in 1924 Fascists murdered the socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti.
The “national community” and who was left out
Nazis promised a Volksgemeinschaft, a “people’s community” beyond class, with holidays, rallies and welfare for its members. Membership was defined by race and loyalty.
Historians agree many Germans felt included and proud; the same community excluded Jews, Roma, disabled people and political opponents, and later robbed and murdered them.

Nazism taught that humanity was divided into superior and inferior races locked in a struggle for survival, a pseudo-science with no basis in biology. Italian Fascism was at first less racial but passed racial laws in 1938.
The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 banned marriage between Jews and other Germans and stripped Jews of citizenship rights; about 400,000 people were forcibly sterilized under a 1933 law.
It drew on “race science” and eugenics that were respected in many countries at the time, including Britain and the United States.
It turned prejudice into law and led directly to forced sterilization and genocide.

Nazism blamed Jews for Germany’s defeat in 1918, for capitalism and for communism at the same time (the myth of “Jewish Bolshevism”). This conspiracy theory was at the centre of Nazi ideology, which the historian Saul Friedländer calls “redemptive antisemitism”.
The 1938 November pogrom (Kristallnacht): synagogues burned across Germany, and about 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps.
A myth: Jews were less than 1% of Germany’s population in 1933, and the claims contradicted each other.

Hitler wanted Lebensraum (“living space”) for Germans in Eastern Europe, to be taken by conquest and emptied of most of its people. Mussolini wanted a new Roman empire in the Mediterranean and Africa. Japan’s militarists proclaimed a “Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere”.
Generalplan Ost (1941–42) planned to expel about 31 million people from Eastern Europe; the Hunger Plan planned to starve tens of millions.
It meant wars of conquest that killed tens of millions and ended in total defeat.
Instead of free unions and strikes, the state would organize employers and workers together into “corporations” for each industry, ending class conflict.
Italy’s Charter of Labour (1927) and Chamber of Fasces and Corporations (1939); in Germany the German Labour Front replaced all free unions in May 1933.
Fascists said they were neither liberal capitalists nor Marxist socialists, but a new force above left and right.
Mussolini had been a leading socialist editor until he was expelled in 1914 for supporting the war.
Debated: see “Left or right?” in Debates.
Critics say the “third way” was a slogan: in power, fascists allied with conservatives and business and destroyed the left.
The word “totalitarian” was coined in Italy in the 1920s, first by opponents, and then adopted proudly by Mussolini and Gentile: a state that controls every part of life.
Hannah Arendt (1951) compared Nazism and Stalinism as two forms of totalitarianism; other historians stress their differences.
Fascism glorified youth, sport and war, and wanted to create a new kind of hard, obedient, warlike person.

About 440,000 Jews deported, mostly to Auschwitz.
Supporters saw alliance with Germany as a way to win back lands lost in 1920.

Authoritarian regime under Pétain, under German pressure and, from November 1942, full German occupation.

Unit 731: about 3,000 killed at its main site; biological attacks on Chinese cities.

He suppressed Portugal’s own fascist movement in 1934, so most scholars call his regime authoritarian rather than fascist. It fought colonial wars in Africa from 1961 until army officers overthrew it in 1974.

Liberalism is the family of ideas that puts individual liberty, equal rights and government by consent at the centre of politics. Born in 17th-century England and the Dutch Republic, it spread through revolutions in America and France and was reshaped in Bengal, Japan, China, Latin America and beyond.

Liberalism changed as it met new conditions: it began against absolute monarchy, added democracy and the welfare state in the industrial age, built a world order after 1945, turned toward markets after the 1970s, and now faces challenges from inside and out.

There is no single founding text for capitalism the way there is for Marxism; it grew out of trade and industry, and thinkers described it as it went. But it changed just as much. Each era rewrote the rules for its own conditions: catch-up countries protected their industries, the Depression brought Keynes, stagflation brought Friedman, and 2008 brought bailouts and a return of industrial policy.

Strikes over hours and wages from the 1830s to today; the eight-hour day was won through it.

Class strongly predicts health, schooling and political power in every society measured. But class conflict is not the only conflict: nation, religion and race often mobilize people more strongly, as in 1914 when most workers followed their nations into war.
Try the Surplus value machine lab: a 10-hour day where 5 hours pay the wage leaves 5 hours of surplus.
Capital, Volume I (1867), especially chapters 1, 7 and 9

Marginalist economists (Jevons, Menger, Walras in the 1870s) explain value by marginal utility. Böhm-Bawerk (1896) argued Marx could not turn labor values into actual prices (the “transformation problem”).
Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts of 1844: “Estranged Labour”
In a market, relations between people (who made something, under what conditions) appear as relations between things (prices). We see a $5 shirt, not the hours and lives inside it.
Hayek (1945): prices compress millions of facts into one number so nobody needs to know them all; that is a feature, not a mask.
Competition forces capitalists to reinvest and grow or die. Capital concentrates into ever bigger firms. Machines replace workers, creating a “reserve army” of unemployed who hold wages down.
From thousands of small car makers in 1910 to a handful of global groups today.

Concentration: largely confirmed (the biggest firms dominate most industries). Rising misery of workers (“immiseration”): not confirmed in rich countries, where real wages rose many times over after 1870.
The 1873 Long Depression, 1929, 2008: crises recur, as Marx predicted.
Capital, Vol. III, part III (published 1894)
Okishio’s theorem (1961) and most mainstream economists dispute the falling-rate law.

Borrowed from Hegel: things change through internal contradictions. A situation produces its opposite, and the clash produces something new. Engels summarized “laws” (quantity into quality, unity of opposites, negation of the negation).
Engels, Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880)
Useful as a habit of looking for tensions and change. As a “science”, critics say it can explain any outcome after the fact, so it predicts nothing.
Mao’s On Contradiction (1937) made it a guide to strategy: find the main contradiction and act on it.
Popper (“What is Dialectic?”, 1940) argued it tolerates contradictions, which makes theories untestable.

The state is not neutral: it is organized force that protects the ruling class’s property. The modern state is “a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie”. Engels traced the state’s origin to the rise of private property and classes.
Governments sending troops against strikers (Pullman Strike 1894, Ludlow 1914).
Engels, The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State (1884)

Between capitalism and communism comes a transition in which the working class rules. Marx’s model was the 1871 Paris Commune: officials elected and recallable at any time, paid workers’ wages, the standing army replaced by armed citizens.
For Marx “dictatorship” meant class rule (as he called parliamentary capitalism a “bourgeois dictatorship”), not necessarily one-man rule. Lenin’s version became one-party rule.
Compare the Commune model with the Leninist states in “Theory vs practice” below: almost none of its features survived.
Kautsky (1918), Luxemburg (1918) and anarchists like Bakunin (1873) warned it would become rule by a party elite over workers.

In the lower phase (later called socialism) people are paid according to work. In the higher phase, with abundance, society can live by “from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs”, classes disappear and the state “withers away”.
Critics: the theory gives no mechanism for the rulers to give up power, so the “transition” becomes permanent.
The ruling ideas of every age are the ideas of its ruling class. People absorb views that serve those in power and treat them as natural. (Engels later used the phrase “false consciousness”.)
Marx and Engels, The German Ideology (1845–46)
Gramsci’s “hegemony” extended it: power rests on consent produced by schools, churches and media, not just force.

Workers left alone develop only “trade-union consciousness” (wanting better wages), Lenin argued. Revolution needs a party of full-time professional revolutionaries, organized like an army, bringing socialist consciousness from outside.

Martov and the Mensheviks (1903) wanted a looser mass party; Trotsky (1904) predicted the party would substitute itself for the class, then the Central Committee for the party, then a dictator for the Central Committee.

Free debate inside the party before a decision, then iron discipline: minorities obey majorities, lower bodies obey higher ones. In 1921, during the Kronstadt revolt, the 10th Congress banned organized factions, and debate shrank to whatever the top allowed.
The rule that made parties effective at seizing and holding power also made them unable to correct their leaders, as the Great Leap famine showed.

Capitalism had reached a monopoly stage where banks and industry merged into finance capital, exported capital abroad and divided the world into colonies. War between empires (1914) followed. Revolution could break the chain at its “weakest link”, such as Russia.
Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism (1916)

Built on J. A. Hobson (1902). Hugely influential in anti-colonial movements from Vietnam to Africa. Critics note capital flowed mostly between rich countries, not to colonies, and many colonies lost money for their rulers.

Written in August–September 1917, it promises a Commune-style state: elected officials paid workers’ wages, armed workers, the state beginning to wither at once. It is Lenin’s most democratic text, written weeks before the Bolsheviks took power and dissolved the elected Constituent Assembly (January 1918).
The gap between this book and the one-party state of 1921 is one of the central debates: betrayal, necessity or the logic of the vanguard idea?

The Cheka (secret police) was founded in December 1917. During the civil war (1918–21) both Reds and Whites used mass terror; the Cheka executed tens of thousands (estimates range widely, roughly 50,000 to over 200,000). Lenin openly defended terror against “class enemies”.
Luxemburg’s critique of Bolshevik terror (1918)
Defenders point to foreign intervention by 14 countries and White atrocities, including pogroms. Critics (Pipes, Figes) see terror as built into Bolshevik theory from the start.

After “war communism” (grain seizures, banned trade) led to famine (about 5 million deaths, 1921–22) and the Kronstadt sailors’ revolt, Lenin restored small private trade and farming in 1921, keeping “commanding heights” (banks, heavy industry, foreign trade) under the state.

In his final notes (December 1922 to January 1923) Lenin warned that Stalin had concentrated “unlimited authority” and should be removed as General Secretary. The letter was suppressed in the USSR until 1956.
Letters to the Congress (“Lenin’s Testament”)
Socialism can come gradually through elections, unions and reforms. Bernstein: “the movement is everything, the final goal nothing”.
Western and Northern Europe; became the welfare state, mostly abandoning Marxism (German SPD’s Bad Godesberg Program, 1959)
Bernstein, Evolutionary Socialism (1899)
Germany; crushed in 1919 when both were murdered by Freikorps troops under a Social Democratic government
Luxemburg, The Russian Revolution (1918)
Vanguard party, one-party state, central planning, collectivized farming, and “socialism in one country”. Stalin wrote it into a fixed doctrine.
Rapid heavy industry and victory in WWII, at the cost of famine, terror and the Gulag; stagnation from the 1970s; collapse 1989–91.
Stalin, The Foundations of Leninism (1924)
Permanent world revolution; the USSR became a “degenerated workers’ state” run by a bureaucratic caste.
Leon Trotsky (murdered on Stalin’s orders, 1940)
Influential critique of Stalinism from the left; critics note Trotsky himself led the Red Army’s terror and crushed Kronstadt.
China 1949–76; inspired the Khmer Rouge, Peru’s Shining Path, Nepal’s Maoists (who later entered elections)

Unified China and raised life expectancy; the Great Leap famine and Cultural Revolution were catastrophes. China’s own party judged his merits primary and his errors secondary (1981), often summarized as 70% right, 30% wrong.
Mao, Report on the Peasant Movement in Hunan (1927)
High growth and open borders for workers to go abroad; one-party rule, the Goli Otok prison camp, inflation and debt in the 1980s; the country broke apart in war (1991–2001).
National self-reliance in ideas, economy and defense; later “military-first” (Songun). Replaced Marxism–Leninism in North Korea’s constitution (references removed 1992–2009).
Most Marxists consider it a nationalist hereditary system rather than Marxism. Survived the USSR’s fall and built nuclear weapons; famine in the 1990s.
Kim Il Sung, “On eliminating dogmatism and formalism and establishing Juche” (1955)
Culture, ideology and consciousness matter as much as economics; power rests on consent (“hegemony”).
Cuba’s revolution survived; most foco guerrillas failed (Guevara was killed in Bolivia, 1967).
Guevara, Socialism and Man in Cuba (1965)
Keep the party’s monopoly on power and state control of key sectors; use markets, private firms and foreign investment to develop productive forces first (“primary stage of socialism”).
Deng Xiaoping, Jiang Zemin, Xi Jinping; Vietnam’s Đổi Mới (1986); Laos
China, Vietnam, Laos; Cuba began adopting parts of it in 2026
Deng, “Emancipate the Mind, Seek Truth From Facts” (1978)

Mostly ratifies decisions made above; the delegate lists are prepared by the leadership. Real contests are rare (the 1934 Soviet “Congress of Victors” vote against Stalin is the famous rumor; most of its delegates were later arrested).
China’s 20th Congress (2022, 2,296 delegates); Vietnam’s 14th (January 2026); North Korea’s 9th (February 2026).
Runs the party between congresses; meets in “plenums” a few times a year.
A club of the most powerful few hundred officials: provincial chiefs, ministers, generals. It can matter in crises (it removed Khrushchev in 1964).
China: 205 full and 171 alternate members after 2022. Vietnam: 180 full members (2026).

The real cabinet. In China the 7-member Politburo Standing Committee is the top; in Vietnam the Politburo (19 members in 2026) traditionally balanced four “pillars” (party chief, state president, prime minister, assembly chair).
Stalin turned it into supreme power because it controlled appointments. Collective leadership rules (China after 1982) limited it; Xi Jinping (2012→) and To Lam (2024→) have re-concentrated power.
Vietnam’s To Lam became both General Secretary and State President in April 2026, like Xi in China.

The heart of the system: the party appoints people to every important job in government, army, state firms, universities and media. Loyalty to superiors, not voters, decides careers. Voslensky estimated about 750,000 Soviet nomenklatura posts.
China’s CCDI; the 2025–26 purge of the Central Military Commission.
Cheka→NKVD→KGB; East Germany’s Stasi (about 91,000 staff and roughly 189,000 informants in 1989); China’s MSS and MPS; Cuba’s MININT.

Assemblies meet briefly and pass what the party proposes, usually unanimously (Vietnam’s 495–0 presidential vote, April 2026). Their committees can still improve laws, and some debate is real in Vietnam’s and China’s legislatures.
Supreme Soviet; China’s NPC (about 2,900 delegates); Vietnam’s National Assembly; Cuba’s National Assembly of People’s Power.
Gosplan (USSR); China’s NDRC and its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–30); Cuba’s JUCEPLAN.
Mass organizations (“transmission belts”)
Lenin called them transmission belts carrying the party’s line to the masses. Independent unions are banned; Poland’s Solidarity (1980) showed what happens when one appears.
China’s eight “democratic parties” and the CPPCC; North Korea’s two minor parties; Vietnam’s Fatherland Front.
Special shops, dachas, cars and hospitals for the elite (Djilas’s “New Class”, 1957). Sankara’s cuts to officials’ pay were a rare exception.
Soviet one-man management from 1918; Yugoslav workers’ councils were the partial exception.
Factions banned 1921; rival socialists jailed or killed.
Communist states fought each other: the Sino-Soviet border clashes (1969), Vietnam vs Cambodia (1978), China vs Vietnam (1979).

When a measure becomes a target, people game it. Soviet nail factories, according to an often-told joke, made tiny nails when judged by count and huge ones when judged by weight. Chinese local officials judged on GDP built empty “ghost” districts. Applies equally to test scores and quarterly earnings.
Firms that know the state will rescue them stop worrying about losses, and demand more inputs. Kornai found this in Hungary; it also describes “too big to fail” banks in 2008.

Bueno de Mesquita and colleagues (2003): leaders survive by rewarding the small group that keeps them in power. In a Leninist state that group is the Central Committee and security chiefs, so leaders buy their loyalty first and the public’s second.

Wintrobe (1998): the more people fear the ruler, the less they tell him the truth, so the ruler cannot know if he is safe or if policies are failing. Great Leap officials reported record harvests during the famine.

Robert Michels (1911) studied the German Social Democratic Party and found every large organization, even a democratic socialist one, is run by a few full-time leaders. Lenin’s vanguard made this a design principle.
A ruler who might be overthrown by a strong deputy has reason to remove strong deputies; deputies know this and hide strength. Stalin’s purges and the 2025–26 PLA purges can be read this way.

Poor countries grow fast by moving workers from farms to factories and copying technology, under any system. Planning can do this quickly (USSR 1930s), but growth slows once catch-up ends unless productivity rises (USSR 1970s; a key question for China now).

The first state founded on Marxism. Took a mostly peasant empire to a nuclear superpower in about 40 years, defeated Nazi Germany at enormous cost, and then stagnated and dissolved peacefully in 1991.
February: the tsar falls. October: Bolsheviks seize power in Petrograd with the slogan “Peace, land, bread”.
Constituent Assembly (where the Bolsheviks won about a quarter of the vote) is dissolved; civil war and foreign intervention begin; the Cheka’s Red Terror.
Kronstadt revolt crushed; factions banned; New Economic Policy restores small markets; famine kills about 5 million.
Lenin dies; Stalin, as General Secretary, outmaneuvers Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev and Bukharin.
First Five-Year Plan and forced collectivization. Famine kills about 5.5–8.7 million (about 3.5–5 million in Ukraine, the Holodomor; about 1.5 million in Kazakhstan).
The Great Terror: about 680,000–750,000 executed according to NKVD records; the Gulag holds over a million.
Nazi invasion; about 27 million Soviet dead; the Red Army takes Berlin.
Brezhnev: stability, cheap housing and jobs, then economic stagnation and invasion of Czechoslovakia (1968) and Afghanistan (1979).
Gorbachev’s glasnost and perestroika; Eastern Europe breaks free in 1989; the USSR dissolves in December 1991.
Literacy rose from about a quarter of the population (1897 census) to near-universal by the 1950s.
Bore the largest share of the land war against Nazi Germany: most German divisions were destroyed on the Eastern Front, at a cost of about 27 million Soviet lives.
Women’s suffrage (1917), legal divorce and abortion (1920), and about half the workforce female by the 1970s.
Life expectancy roughly doubled from about 30 (around 1900) to about 68–69 by the 1960s, near US levels, before stalling.
Famines: about 5 million dead in 1921–22, 5.5–8.7 million in 1932–33 (including about 3.5–5 million in Ukraine, recognized by Ukraine and over 30 countries as genocide) and 1–1.5 million in 1946–47.
The Great Terror of 1937–38: about 680,000–750,000 people shot, by the NKVD’s own records.
The Gulag: about 18 million passed through 1930–53; about 1.5–1.8 million deaths are documented in camp records, with higher estimates including those released to die.
Deportations of entire nations (Chechens, Crimean Tatars, Volga Germans and others), with very high death rates.
Chronic shortages, environmental disasters (Aral Sea, Chernobyl 1986), and occupation of Eastern Europe.
Heroic construction of socialism; Stalin’s crimes admitted after 1956 as “errors” of a personality cult.
The scale of famine and terror, hidden until the archives opened.
Post-1991 archival historians (Davies, Wheatcroft, Khlevniuk, Applebaum, Kotkin)
Archives confirmed mass repression but narrowed some inflated Cold War estimates; debates continue over intent in the famine.
Repression memory groups like Memorial were dissolved by court order (2021).
Gone since 1991. Its successors range from democratic Baltic states to authoritarian Russia and Belarus.

Davies & Wheatcroft, The Years of Hunger (2004); Khlevniuk, The History of the Gulag (2004); Applebaum, Gulag (2003); Kotkin, Stalin (2014–17); Allen, Farm to Factory (2003); Maddison Project Database

Ruled by the Communist Party since 1949, with about 100 million members. Went through Mao’s revolution and catastrophes, then Deng’s market reforms, and now Xi Jinping’s re-centralization. It is the world’s second-largest economy and the most important living test of whether a Leninist party can run a market economy.
Communist Party founded in Shanghai by about a dozen delegates representing roughly 50 members.
Nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek massacre communists in Shanghai; the party retreats to the countryside.
War against Japan; the party grows from about 40,000 to over a million members.
Land reform redistributes land; estimates of landlords killed range from about 1 to 2 million or more. Korean War.
Hundred Flowers invites criticism, then the Anti-Rightist Campaign labels about 550,000 people “rightists”.
Great Leap Forward: backyard steel furnaces, communes, false harvest reports. Famine kills an estimated 15–55 million; most demographers estimate 30–45 million.
Cultural Revolution: Red Guards, persecution of teachers and officials; an estimated 1–2 million deaths.
Third Plenum under Deng Xiaoping: reform and opening. Collective farms dissolved into household contracts; Special Economic Zones (Shenzhen) open in 1980.
The party’s Resolution on History: Mao’s merits primary, his errors secondary (popularly “70% right, 30% wrong”); the Cultural Revolution was a catastrophe.
Tiananmen protests crushed on June 4; deaths range from several hundred to several thousand, still officially unacknowledged.
Deng’s Southern Tour restarts reform: “socialist market economy”.
Xi begins a third term as General Secretary at the 20th Congress.
Fourth Plenum adopts recommendations for the 15th Five-Year Plan; CMC Vice Chair He Weidong, Admiral Miao Hua and seven other generals expelled. (developing)

January: Zhang Youxia, the top uniformed officer, and Joint Staff chief Liu Zhenli placed under investigation, leaving the CMC with Xi and Zhang Shengmin. March 12: the National People’s Congress approves the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026–30), prioritizing technological self-reliance. (developing)

Xi Jinping holds the three top posts: General Secretary (party), Chairman of the Central Military Commission (army) and State President. The 7-member Politburo Standing Committee, the Organization Department’s control of appointments, party committees inside government, firms and universities, the CCDI’s discipline system and the United Front Work Department make the party the center of everything
Life expectancy rose from roughly 35–40 in 1949 to about 65 by 1978 (under Mao) and about 78 today.
The World Bank estimates close to 800 million people left extreme poverty since 1980, about three-quarters of the global reduction in that period.
GDP grew around 9–10% a year from 1978 to the 2010s, the fastest sustained growth of a large economy recorded.
The Great Leap famine, the largest in recorded history.
Repression in Xinjiang and Tibet, Hong Kong’s 2020 National Security Law, pervasive censorship and surveillance.
Severe pollution (improving since 2013), high inequality, a household registration (hukou) system that limits rural migrants’ rights, and a property-sector crisis since 2021.
A century of struggle that ended national humiliation, built socialism with Chinese characteristics and achieved a “moderately prosperous society”; mistakes were corrected by the party itself.
The famine’s scale, Tiananmen, and the fact that no outside force can correct the party.
That most Chinese people say they are satisfied with the central government (Harvard Ash Center surveys, 2003–16), and the scale of real poverty reduction.

Developing in 2026: slower growth (official 2026 target 4.5–5%), a property slump, competition with the US over technology, and the deepest military purge since the Cultural Revolution. The 15th Five-Year Plan bets on technology self-reliance.

A revolution against the US-backed dictator Fulgencio Batista turned Marxist–Leninist by 1961 and allied with the USSR. Known for literacy, doctors and health statistics and for one-party rule and emigration. In 2026 it faces its worst crisis since the 1990s.
Fidel Castro’s failed attack on the Moncada barracks; his trial speech “History Will Absolve Me”.
Nationalization of US property; US embargo begins; Bay of Pigs invasion fails (1961); Castro declares the revolution socialist; Cuban Missile Crisis (1962).
Literacy campaign: about 250,000 volunteers; official illiteracy falls from about 24% to about 4% in one year.
Cuban troops in Angola fight South African forces; both sides claim victory at Cuito Cuanavale (1988), which is followed by talks on Namibian independence.
“Special Period” after Soviet aid ends: GDP falls about a third, widespread hunger.
Raúl Castro succeeds Fidel; limited private businesses allowed; 2019 constitution approved by referendum.
July 11 protests across the island; hundreds imprisoned.

A US oil blockade since January brings repeated island-wide blackouts (at least six by September). Díaz-Canel confirms talks with Washington and in June admits problems that do not come from the embargo, calling for urgent market reforms; on June 18 the National Assembly approves more than 175 of them. (developing)

The Communist Party of Cuba is constitutionally the “superior leading force”. First Secretary and President Miguel Díaz-Canel, the Political Bureau, and the armed forces, whose GAESA conglomerate controls much of the hard-currency economy. CDRs on every block, MININT security services. National Assembly candidates are vetted by commissions; there is one candidate per seat.
The 1961 literacy campaign: about 700,000 adults taught to read in one year by volunteer teachers, many of them teenagers.
Lower income inequality than most of Latin America in the 1980s; strong record against racial segregation laws compared with pre-1959 Cuba.
Political prisoners and executions (hundreds to several thousand in the early years, numbers disputed); no free press or competitive elections.
Chronic shortages, rationing (libreta) since 1962, and economic dependence first on the USSR, then on Venezuela.
Emigration of a large share of the population since 1959.
Health data are contested: researchers argue infant mortality is understated by reclassifying deaths (Berdine et al., 2018).
A small nation that defended its independence and social gains against a 60-year US blockade.
Its own economic mistakes, as Díaz-Canel himself said in June 2026.
That pre-1959 prosperity was concentrated, and that US sanctions have real effects on Cubans.

Developing in 2026: daily blackouts and fuel shortages under a US oil blockade, talks with Washington, and reported US pressure for Díaz-Canel to leave. In June the National Assembly approved more than 175 market reforms, including larger private firms and private banks, while leaders insist Cuba is not giving up socialism.

Soviet occupation north of the 38th parallel; Kim Il Sung installed; land reform and nationalizations.
“August Faction Incident”: pro-Soviet and pro-Chinese rivals purged after criticizing Kim’s personality cult.
Juche declared; rapid postwar rebuilding; North Korea probably richer than the South until about the early 1970s.
Kim Il Sung dies; famine after Soviet aid ends and floods. Estimates range from about 240,000 to 3.5 million deaths; demographic studies suggest roughly 600,000–1 million.
Kim Jong Il: “military-first” politics; first nuclear test (2006).
South Korea declared a separate “hostile state”; reunification dropped. Treaty with Russia; troops sent to fight Ukraine (2024–25).
Ninth Party Congress (February 19–25) re-elects Kim Jong Un as General Secretary and confirms the nuclear line. (developing)

Kim Jong Un as General Secretary of the Workers’ Party of Korea and President of State Affairs; Politburo Presidium; the Organization and Guidance Department; the Korean People’s Army; Ministry of State Security; songbun hereditary loyalty classes that decide where families can live and work. See the North Korea section of “Who really rules?” for detail.
The 1990s famine; ongoing chronic malnutrition (UN agencies).
Political prison camps holding an estimated 80,000–120,000 people (UN Commission of Inquiry, 2014).
The US bombing campaign of 1950–53 that still shapes North Korean fears.
Developing in 2026: closer military ties with Russia, three straight years of reported growth (from arms trade, per South Korean estimates), no talks with the US or South.

A communist-led national liberation movement that defeated France (1954) and the United States (1975), reunified the country, failed with Soviet-style planning, and then grew fast after market reforms (Đổi Mới, 1986). In 2026 power is more concentrated than at any time in decades.
Land reform in the North; thousands executed (estimates about 13,500 to over 15,000); the party later admitted errors.
War against the US-backed South and the US; about 2–3 million Vietnamese dead.
Reunification; re-education camps for southern officials; collectivization in the South fails; hundreds of thousands of “boat people” flee; war with Cambodia and China.
“Blazing furnace” anti-corruption campaign under Nguyễn Phú Trọng; presidents and ministers forced out.
Massive state restructuring: provinces merged from 63 to 34 and the district level abolished; ministries cut.
January: 14th Congress re-elects To Lam as General Secretary. April 7: the National Assembly elects him State President by 495–0, ending the old “four pillars” power-sharing. (developing)

The Communist Party of Vietnam (about 5–6 million members), Politburo and Secretariat, a Central Military Commission, and the Ministry of Public Security (which To Lam headed 2016–24). The Fatherland Front groups mass organizations. The National Assembly is more active in debate than China’s NPC, but candidates are vetted.
Poverty fell from about half the population in the early 1990s to a few percent by World Bank measures.
The postwar failures until 1986 and the land reform killings.
Developing in 2026: To Lam holds both top posts, like Xi; the state has been reorganized; the economy is caught between US tariffs and Chinese competition.

Two different stories joined by one name. Thomas Sankara, a Marxist and pan-Africanist army captain, led a four-year revolution (1983–87) with remarkable social programs and real repression before he was assassinated. Captain Ibrahim Traoré, in power since a 2022 coup, uses Sankara’s image but runs a military government without a Marxist–Leninist party, and has abolished political parties.
August 4: Sankara takes power in a coup backed by left-wing officers and civilian groups; National Council of the Revolution.

Country renamed Burkina Faso (“land of upright people”). Mass vaccination of about 2.5 million children in two weeks; officials’ salaries cut and government Mercedes fleet sold; tree planting; campaigns against female genital cutting and forced marriage (female genital cutting was made a crime only in 1996).
Committees for the Defense of the Revolution become abusive; teachers who strike are fired (about 1,400); trade unions repressed; Popular Revolutionary Tribunals try former officials.
July: speech to the Organization of African Unity urging a united refusal to pay debt. October 15: Sankara killed in a coup that brings his comrade Blaise Compaoré to power for 27 years.
Jihadist insurgency spreads from Mali; by 2024 over two million people displaced.
April: a military tribunal convicts Compaoré in absentia for Sankara’s murder (life sentence).
Two coups; Captain Ibrahim Traoré seizes power on September 30.
French troops expelled; ties with Russia; Alliance (then Confederation) of Sahel States with Mali and Niger; withdrawal from ECOWAS; transition extended to 2029.
January 29: decree dissolves all political parties. January: government says it foiled a coup plot. April: Traoré tells Burkinabè to “forget” democracy. (developing)
Sankara era: no elections, repression of unions and critics, executions after a coup plot (1984).

Traoré era: massacres of civilians by soldiers and militias documented by Human Rights Watch; journalists and critics conscripted or detained; parties abolished; the insurgency still controls large areas.
Sankara was Africa’s Che, killed for challenging France and debt; Traoré continues his fight.
Much viral content about Traoré online is false or AI-made; e.g. Burkina Faso has been in an IMF program since 2023 despite claims it rejected the IMF.

Developing in 2026: parties dissolved, transition to 2029, war with jihadist groups, reported coup plots, alliance with Mali and Niger. Ask of Traoré the same questions as of any ruler: how can he be removed, and who checks him?

The communist state that broke with Stalin (1948) and tried a different model: workers’ self-management, markets and non-alignment. It was more open and prosperous than the Soviet bloc, but it was still a one-party state, and it broke apart in war.
Open borders: about a million work in West Germany and elsewhere; 1974 constitution decentralizes to republics.
Tito dies; foreign debt, inflation and unemployment; nationalism rises.
Breakup wars: about 130,000–140,000 dead; genocide at Srebrenica (1995).
High growth in the 1950s–70s; consumer goods and travel freedom unusual in the communist world.
Self-managed firms borrowed heavily and resisted cutting jobs; inflation reached over 1,000% in 1989.
Unresolved national tensions exploded after 1990.
Shared prosperity and peace for 45 years.

About 2.7–3 million people leave for the West.
The Berlin Wall is built; at least 140 people die at it by 1989.
Mass protests (“We are the people”) and the fall of the Wall on November 9.
SED Politburo; the Stasi with about 91,000 staff and about 189,000 unofficial informants in 1989; bloc parties under the National Front.
Living standards well below West Germany: estimates of GDP per head range roughly from one-third to under two-thirds of West Germany’s by 1989.
Real social provision that many East Germans missed after 1990 (“Ostalgie”).
Reunified since 1990; eastern Germany still has lower wages and different voting patterns.

Disease and starvation in camps; desert expulsion.

The continuity between colonial violence and later genocide (Arendt, Césaire, Zimmerer).

From the Seneca Falls Convention (1848) to the vote in New Zealand (1893), Finland (1906), Britain (1918/1928), the US (1920) and beyond.

Mass conscript armies of millions; whole economies mobilized; rationing and hunger (the British blockade caused hunger-related deaths in Germany: a German government report in 1918 claimed about 763,000; modern historians estimate roughly 400,000–500,000). About 15–22 million dead including civilians. Four empires collapsed (Russian, German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman). Socialist parties that had promised to oppose war mostly voted for it in 1914.
A tragedy of statesmen; conservatives later mourned the lost world of before 1914.
The collapse of the Second International in 1914 split the left: majority socialists backed national war efforts; a minority opposed.
Lenin: an imperialist war for the redivision of the world among capitalist powers; “turn the imperialist war into a civil war.”

The war destroyed four empires and killed millions.
Most socialist parties voted for war credits in 1914.

In February 1917 strikes and mutinies toppled the tsar. In October the Bolsheviks seized power under Lenin, closed the elected Constituent Assembly (January 1918), made peace with Germany and won a brutal civil war against the Whites.
War defeats, hunger, land-hungry peasants, a weak provisional government that kept fighting, and a disciplined Bolshevik party with a clear slogan: “Peace, land and bread.”

Civil war, Red and White terror, and famine killed perhaps 7–12 million. The Cheka (secret police) was founded in December 1917. War communism gave way to the NEP market compromise in 1921. The USSR was founded in 1922.
The fulfilment of conservative warnings about revolution; Churchill wanted to “strangle Bolshevism in its cradle.”

For Leninists, the first workers’ revolution, defending itself against “14 invading armies” and the Whites (a Soviet-era count: most foreign contingents were small and stayed at the edges, except Japan’s roughly 70,000 troops in Siberia); Trotskyists say it degenerated only later under Stalin.
Fascists and Nazis cast Bolshevism as the mortal enemy, and the Nazis falsely portrayed it as a Jewish conspiracy (“Judeo-Bolshevism”), a myth central to their propaganda.
Anarchists supported the revolution at first and were then crushed (Kronstadt 1921, Makhno in Ukraine); Emma Goldman wrote My Disillusionment in Russia.

Britain, France, the US, Japan (about 70,000 troops in Siberia) and others sent troops and supplies to the anti-Bolshevik side; historians debate how much it mattered, and Soviet propaganda made it central.
Versailles, the new nations and the 1918–23 upheavals

The Paris Peace Conference created new states (Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia), the League of Nations, and harsh terms for Germany. Revolutions swept Germany (1918–19) and Hungary (1919). The Ottoman Arab lands became British and French mandates; China’s May Fourth Movement protested Japan’s gains.
Influenza killed tens of millions worldwide (1918–20). Germany faced reparations and then hyperinflation (1923).
Germany’s Weimar Republic was born from defeat; the Spartacist uprising was crushed and Luxemburg and Liebknecht murdered by Freikorps soldiers (1919).
German nationalists spread the “stab in the back” myth that the army was betrayed by socialists and Jews; Hitler built his movement on rejecting Versailles.

Hyperinflation peaked in late 1923 with prices doubling every few days.

Mussolini, a former socialist editor, founded the Fascist movement in 1919. Squads of blackshirts attacked socialists, unions and peasant leagues. After the March on Rome (1922) the king appointed him prime minister; by 1926 he ruled as dictator.
Postwar crisis, the “Two Red Years” of factory occupations (1919–20), veteran anger at a “mutilated victory”, and elites who preferred fascism to socialism.

One-party rule, the murder of socialist deputy Giacomo Matteotti (1924), corporatism, the Lateran Pacts with the Church (1929), invasion of Ethiopia (1935–36) with poison gas, racial laws (1938), alliance with Hitler, defeat and civil war (1943–45).
Liberals like Croce at first tolerated fascism as a barrier to socialism, then opposed it; it destroyed every liberal freedom.
Many conservatives, the monarchy, the Church hierarchy, landowners and industrialists backed or accepted fascism as a defense of order and property.
Fascism was a counter-revolution against the workers’ movement: its first victims were socialists and unions.
Marxists (Gramsci, later Dimitrov) saw fascism as the dictatorship of the most reactionary elements of capital, mobilizing a frightened middle class.
Fascists said they offered a “third way” beyond capitalism and communism: national rebirth, discipline, a corporate state and empire.
Fascist squads used systematic violence against the left before taking power.

Fear of foreign attack, ideological hostility to private peasants (“kulaks”), the goal of building socialism in one country fast, and Stalin’s personal power.
Peasants killed livestock rather than surrender them; grain was requisitioned and exported; the famine regions were sealed off.

The USSR became an industrial and military power that later bore the brunt of defeating Germany; famine deaths about 5.5–8.7 million in 1932–33 (3.5–5 million in Ukraine); about 18 million passed through the Gulag.
Proof that central planning and one-party rule lead to mass murder (Conquest, Applebaum).
Stalinists defended collectivization as necessary to industrialize before the war; Trotskyists called the regime a degenerated workers’ state; many Western Marxists broke with Moscow after 1956.
Nazi propaganda used Soviet crimes to justify its war of annihilation in the East, while committing its own.
The confirmation of Bakunin’s warning that a “red bureaucracy” would rule.

The Depression, Versailles resentment, fear of communism, the street violence of the SA, propaganda, divisions on the left (the KPD called the SPD “social fascists”), and elite miscalculation.
Six million unemployed in 1932; failing banks; a deadlocked parliament ruling by emergency decree.

The SPD voted against the Enabling Act, the only party present to do so (the communist deputies had already been arrested, had fled or were barred); social democrats were imprisoned and murdered.

Ghettos, starvation, deportation by railway, industrialized killing.
The Nuremberg trials, the Genocide Convention (1948), the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948), and the founding of Israel (1948).

The People’s Republic of China; the Korean War killed about 3 million and divided Korea, setting up the starkest experiment in modern history.

For Maoists, the liberation of the Chinese people from feudalism and imperialism; China “stood up”.

The fastest growth Western Europe, North America and Japan have ever had, with falling inequality: rebuilding, mass production, cheap oil, strong unions, high top tax rates, welfare states and Keynesian demand management. West Germany and Japan had “economic miracles.”
