Cuba had relatively high income for Latin America in 1958 but great rural poverty.
A communist base 90 miles from Florida; Cuban exiles became a pillar of American conservatism.
Cuba has had high literacy and life expectancy and no competitive elections since 1959.

Brown v. Board (1954), the Montgomery bus boycott, sit-ins, the March on Washington (1963), the Civil Rights Act (1964) and Voting Rights Act (1965) ended legal segregation. The 1960s also brought second-wave feminism, the anti-war movement and the 1968 protests worldwide.
Many conservatives opposed the 1964 Act on states’ rights or property grounds (Goldwater); today most claim Martin Luther King’s colorblind ideal.
White supremacists bombed churches and murdered activists; segregationists like Wallace built a populist backlash.
Black voter registration in Mississippi rose from about 7% (1964) to about 60% (1968).

After defeating France (1954), Ho Chi Minh’s communists sought to unify Vietnam. The reunification elections promised for 1956 by the Geneva Accords were never held: South Vietnam’s government and the US opposed them, partly because they expected Ho to win. The US backed South Vietnam and sent over 500,000 troops after the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution (1964). Saigon fell in 1975.
Anti-colonial nationalism fused with communism; US containment and the “domino theory”.

Before: nearly a century of French colonial rule, rubber plantations and heavy taxes; a famine in 1944–45 under Japanese and French control killed perhaps 1–2 million; land owned by a small elite. During: massive bombing (more tonnage than in WWII), napalm and Agent Orange.
About 2–3 million Vietnamese and 58,000 Americans dead; re-education camps and “boat people” after 1975; Vietnam later adopted market reforms (Doi Moi, 1986).

After a failed coup attempt blamed on the Communist Party (PKI), the army and allied militias killed an estimated 500,000–1,000,000 alleged communists. US, British and Australian officials knew and supported the army; US diplomats handed over lists of communist names (first reported in 1990), and US embassy cables declassified in 2017 show officials followed the killings in detail. General Suharto
One of the largest mass killings of the century, with Western governments providing lists and support (documented in declassified files); Suharto’s “New Order” brought growth and dictatorship.
A massacre of the world’s third-largest communist party.

Nixon ended the dollar’s convertibility into gold (1971), ending Bretton Woods. OPEC’s embargo (1973) quadrupled oil prices; the Iranian revolution doubled them again (1979). Inflation and unemployment rose together; Volcker’s Fed raised rates to about 20% (1981) to break inflation.
US inflation peaked near 14% (1980); unemployment near 11% (1982).
Inflation in the US was finally brought down by tight money in 1979–83.

Salvador Allende, an elected Marxist, nationalized copper and banks. With the economy in crisis and the US working to destabilize him, General Pinochet’s coup (September 11, 1973) installed a dictatorship that killed about 3,200 people and tortured tens of thousands. Free-market reforms followed.
Inflation over 300% in 1973; shortages and strikes.
After a 1982 crash, Chile grew fast and became Latin America’s richest country per person by some measures; it returned to democracy after a 1988 plebiscite.
The overthrow of democratic socialism by force; Allende’s death is a martyrdom.
The dictatorship killed about 3,200 and tortured about 40,000 according to Chilean commissions.
Was the Chilean “miracle” due to markets or did it happen despite the dictatorship?
Most economists credit market reforms and later democratic governments; critics stress the 1982 crash, inequality and repression.

The Khmer Rouge emptied cities, abolished money and schools, and forced the population into agricultural labor camps. About 1.5–2 million people, roughly a quarter of the population, died from execution, starvation and disease.

Extreme agrarian communist ideology; a 1970 coup that put a pro-US general in power and dragged Cambodia into the Vietnam War; US bombing (about 500,000 tons in 1969–73) that devastated the countryside and helped Khmer Rouge recruitment; Chinese backing; and paranoid purges. Vietnam invaded and ended the regime in 1979, yet the US, China and others kept a Khmer Rouge-led coalition in Cambodia’s UN
Vietnam invaded and ended the regime (1979); China and the US later backed the Khmer Rouge’s UN seat against Vietnam.
Cambodia was a victim of great-power politics before, during and after.
About a quarter of Cambodia’s population died.

After Mao, Deng let farmers sell surplus crops, opened Special Economic Zones, welcomed foreign investment and allowed private business, while keeping one-party rule (“socialism with Chinese characteristics”).
The failures of Maoism, the example of East Asian “tigers”, and pragmatism (“it doesn’t matter if a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice”).
In 1978 most Chinese lived in rural poverty.
About 800 million people left extreme poverty; China became the largest manufacturing economy; inequality and pollution soared.
Extreme poverty fell dramatically in China after 1978.

A broad revolution toppled the Shah; Ayatollah Khomeini’s Islamists took control, founding an Islamic Republic. The Iran–Iraq War (1980–88) killed perhaps 500,000+. The USSR invaded Afghanistan (1979); US, Saudi and Pakistani support for the mujahideen helped force Soviet withdrawal (1989).
The Shah’s repression, inequality and Westernization, the 1953 coup’s legacy, clerical networks; Soviet fear of losing a client state.
A popular revolution captured by theocrats; liberals and leftists who joined it were later executed or exiled.
Thousands of leftist and other political prisoners were executed in 1988.

Thatcher (1979) and Reagan (1981) cut taxes on top incomes, fought unions (the 1984–85 miners’ strike, the 1981 air traffic controllers), privatized industries and deregulated finance. The “Washington Consensus” spread these policies via the IMF and World Bank.
Stagflation, union militancy (the 1978–79 Winter of Discontent), and the intellectual work of Hayek, Friedman and think tanks.
Structural adjustment programs imposed austerity on indebted poor countries in the 1980s–90s.
Top income shares rose strongly in the US and UK after 1980.
Top marginal tax rates fell sharply after 1980.
When US interest rates soared, heavily indebted countries could not pay. Mexico defaulted in 1982; a “lost decade” of falling incomes, hyperinflation and austerity followed.
Petrodollar lending in the 1970s, Volcker rate hikes, falling commodity prices.
IMF programs and the Washington Consensus; the Brady Plan (1989) restructured debt.
1989 and the collapse of the Soviet Union

Poland’s Solidarity union (1980) challenged communist rule; Gorbachev’s glasnost and perestroika loosened controls; in 1989 communist regimes fell across Eastern Europe, mostly peacefully, and the Berlin Wall opened. China crushed the Tiananmen protests (June 1989). The USSR dissolved in December 1991.
Soviet growth near zero in the 1980s; queues; the Chernobyl disaster (1986).
Fukuyama’s “end of history”: liberal democracy had defeated its rivals.
Marxist-Leninists blame betrayal by Gorbachev; other Marxists say it proved Soviet “state socialism” was never socialism.
Anarchists see the end of the most powerful “workers’ state” as confirmation that it was a new ruling class.

Russia freed prices overnight (1992) and sold state enterprises through vouchers and the “loans for shares” deals that created oligarchs. Output fell by about 40%, life expectancy for men dropped below 58, and Russia defaulted in 1998.
Hyperinflation (over 2,000% in 1992), unpaid wages, mafia violence.
Vladimir Putin rose in 1999–2000 promising order; oil revenues brought recovery in the 2000s along with re-centralized power.
Russian conservatives see the 1990s as national humiliation by the West; Putin’s appeal rests on that memory.
Male life expectancy fell sharply in the early 1990s.

Yugoslavia broke up in wars marked by ethnic cleansing; Bosnian Serb forces murdered about 8,000 Bosniak men and boys at Srebrenica (1995). In Rwanda, Hutu extremists murdered about 500,000–800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu in about 100 days (1994).
Nationalist politicians exploiting collapse (Milošević, Tudjman), economic crisis; in Rwanda, a racialized colonial legacy, civil war and organized propaganda (radio RTLM).
International criminal tribunals; the doctrine of a “responsibility to protect”; NATO intervention in Bosnia (1995) and Kosovo (1999).
Ethno-nationalists produced the ideology of ethnic cleansing; their crimes are documented by international courts.
Srebrenica and the Rwandan killings were ruled genocide by international courts.
Nelson Mandela was released (1990) after 27 years in prison; negotiations ended apartheid; the first democratic election (1994) made him president.
Western conservatives (Thatcher, Reagan) opposed sanctions and called the ANC terrorist at the time.

India liberalized (1991), NAFTA (1994) and the WTO (1995) lowered trade barriers, the EU created the euro (1999) and expanded east (2004), China joined the WTO (2001), and the internet connected the world.

Global extreme poverty fell from about 38% (1990) to under 10% (2019); rich-country manufacturing towns lost jobs (Autor, Dorn and Hanson estimate China-related losses of about 1–2 million US manufacturing jobs in 1999–2011).
Asia’s rise shifted the center of the world economy back toward where it was before 1800.
Branko Milanović’s “elephant curve” shows big gains for the global middle and the top, stagnation for rich-country working classes.
Share of people below $1.90 a day since 1820.
Currency pegs collapsed under capital flight; IMF rescues came with austerity. Indonesia’s economy shrank about 13% and Suharto fell.

Al-Qaeda killed nearly 3,000 people on September 11, 2001. The US invaded Afghanistan (2001) and Iraq (2003, on false claims of weapons of mass destruction). The Islamic State rose in 2014. US forces left Afghanistan in 2021 as the Taliban returned.
Mass surveillance (Patriot Act), Guantánamo and torture programs.
Brown University’s Costs of War project estimates over 900,000 direct deaths and trillions of dollars spent.
Liberal internationalists split: some supported spreading democracy, others condemned torture and surveillance.
Most of the left opposed the Iraq war (massive protests in 2003).

A US housing bubble financed by subprime mortgages and complex securities burst; Lehman Brothers failed (September 2008); governments bailed out banks and central banks cut rates to zero. Greece and others nearly defaulted in the euro crisis (2010–12) and faced austerity.
US unemployment hit 10%; millions of foreclosures; Greek unemployment over 25%.
Bailing out banks while ordinary people lost homes showed whose side the system was on (Occupy: “We are the 99%”).
Unemployment in Greece and Spain exceeded 25%.

Mass protests toppled rulers in Tunisia, Egypt, Libya and Yemen (2011). Only Tunisia became a democracy, for a time. Syria’s uprising became a civil war (over 500,000 dead, 13 million displaced); Assad fell in December 2024.
Counter-revolution in Egypt (2013 coup), state collapse in Libya and Yemen, refugee flows into Europe (2015).
European far-right parties grew on the 2015 refugee crisis.

Britain voted to leave the EU (2016); Donald Trump won the US presidency (2016) and again (2024); populist and national-conservative leaders rose in Hungary, Poland, Brazil, Italy, India and elsewhere. Left populists (Podemos, Syriza, Sanders, Corbyn) also surged.
Deindustrialization and the China shock, the 2008 crisis, immigration, cultural backlash, social media, distrust of elites.
Rising tariffs and immigration restrictions; V-Dem records democratic backsliding in Hungary and elsewhere; the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol.
Capitalist crisis producing both left and right revolts, as in the 1930s.

After Ukraine’s Maidan revolution (2014), Russia annexed Crimea and backed separatists in the Donbas. In February 2022 Russia launched a full-scale invasion. Ukraine stopped the advance on Kyiv; a war of attrition followed. In 2025–26 the US pushed for peace talks, including meetings in Abu Dhabi in November 2026 (developing).

Before: Ukraine was divided over closer ties to Russia or the EU, with a large Russian-speaking population and deep corruption; NATO had promised in 2008 that Ukraine would one day join; in 2014 protests drove out a pro-Russian president. During: the largest war in Europe since 1945; millions of refugees; energy and food price shocks.
Hundreds of thousands of military casualties on both sides (estimates vary and are disputed); Finland and Sweden joined NATO; Europe rearmed.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.
A new coronavirus emerged in Wuhan, China (late 2019). Lockdowns shut economies; vaccines were developed in under a year. The WHO estimates about 15 million excess deaths in 2020–21.
Massive government spending, followed by an inflation surge (2021–23); deep polarization over lockdowns, masks and vaccines.
Rich countries hoarded vaccines early (“vaccine apartheid”).

The IPCC (1988) concluded human emissions are warming the planet. The Paris Agreement (2015) set a goal of well below 2°C. Solar, wind and batteries became the cheapest new power in most places; global temperatures reached about 1.5°C above pre-industrial in 2024.

Xi centralized power, removed term limits (2018), repressed Uyghurs in Xinjiang and crushed Hong Kong’s autonomy (2020). The US and China moved from engagement to rivalry: tariffs (from 2018), chip export controls, and tension over Taiwan.
A “new Cold War” debate; supply chains shifting; arms buildups in the Pacific.

Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023 killed about 1,200 people in Israel and took about 250 hostages. Israel’s war in Gaza killed over 71,000 Palestinians according to the Gaza Health Ministry, destroyed most of the territory and caused famine conditions. A US-brokered ceasefire began October 10, 2025 and has been fragile (developing).

Before: about 2 million people, most descended from 1948 refugees, lived in Gaza under an Israeli and Egyptian blockade since 2007, with very high unemployment and repeated wars (2008–09, 2014, 2021); Hamas ruled Gaza and rejected Israel’s existence; Israelis lived with rocket fire. During: most of Gaza’s people displaced; hospitals destroyed.
The International Court of Justice is hearing South Africa’s genocide case; the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli and Hamas leaders (2024).
The October 7 attack killed about 1,200 people, most of them civilians.
Tens of thousands of Palestinians, a large share of them women and children, have been killed.

Deep learning and large language models (ChatGPT, 2022, and its rivals, including the AI you are using) spread rapidly; investment in chips and data centers became the largest technology boom since the internet.

President Trump’s second term brought sweeping tariffs under emergency powers; in February 2026 the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that the IEEPA tariffs were unlawful. On February 28, 2026, US and Israeli strikes on Iran began a war in which Supreme Leader Khamenei was killed; a ceasefire mediated by Pakistan in April was followed by later breakdowns. US forces captured Venezuela’s Nicolás Maduro in Jan
Economic nationalism and executive power, Middle East rivalry and the Iranian nuclear program, US policy toward Venezuela, voter reaction.
Concerned about tariffs, executive power and the international order; welcomed the Supreme Court’s check.
Same people, same culture, split in 1945. Liberals cite this as the cleanest natural experiment.

There are no reliable North Korean figures for 1945–1990 (the gap in the chart); most estimates say the North was richer and more industrial until around the 1970s; the South was a dictatorship until 1987 with heavy state industrial policy.
Another split nation: watch steel and military capabilities; incomes differed by roughly 2–3 times by 1989.
Soviet growth: impressive or a dead end?
Marxists point to fast growth from 1928 to the 1960s; liberals point to stagnation after 1970.
Both Mao-era foundations (literacy, health) and post-1978 reforms matter.
Liberals cite the fall in extreme poverty since 1820 as capitalism’s achievement.
Critics (Hickel) argue the $1.90 line is too low and that much of the decline is China; defenders reply the trend holds at higher lines too. Switch to the $10 line and compare.
Piketty: wars, taxes and unions compressed inequality; it rose again after 1980.
How many people live under each regime type since 1800.
Pinker argues violence has declined since 1945; critics (Taleb, Braumoeller) say big wars are rare and unpredictable.
Hereditary succession to the eldest male line (Salic law). Offices were often bought and inherited (“venality of office”).
No national elections. The Estates-General, an advisory assembly of the three estates, did not meet between 1614 and 1789. Villages had some local assemblies.
The parlements register it; they could issue “remonstrances” (objections).
Censorship, lettres de cachet (imprisonment without trial, e.g. in the Bastille), persecution of Protestants after 1685.
Repeated wars produced crushing debt. When the crown could not borrow more in 1788, it had to summon the Estates-General, which turned into the Revolution.

General elections at least every five years, first past the post. Also local elections, devolved parliaments in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, occasional referendums (Brexit 2016), petitions, unions, protest.

Market economy with a large state: the Treasury sets taxes and spending; the Bank of England (independent since 1997) sets interest rates. Postwar governments nationalized key industries (1945–51); Thatcher privatized them (1980s).
Gradual expansion of the vote (1832, 1867, 1884, 1918, 1928), welfare state and NHS (1948), devolution (1999).
Legal opposition; “His Majesty’s Most Loyal Opposition” has an official role and funding.
One of the most stable democracies; critics note first past the post can give large majorities on minority votes (e.g. 2024: Labour won about 63% of seats on about 34% of the vote).
Critics call it an “elective dictatorship” (Lord Hailsham’s phrase) with weak checks between elections and a disproportionate voting system.

Power is deliberately divided: between the federal government and 50 states (federalism), and within the federal government among Congress, the president and the courts (separation of powers with checks and balances). A written constitution, amended 27 times, is the supreme law.

Formally divided among the three branches. In practice, presidents have grown more powerful (executive orders, emergency powers, war powers), the Supreme Court decides many central questions, and money, interest groups and the two major parties shape what reaches the agenda.

Federal elections every two years; thousands of state and local offices; ballot initiatives in many states; primaries; jury service; lobbying, petitions, protest and the courts. Turnout is lower than in many democracies (about 66% in 2020, a high).
Senate floor vote (most bills need 60 votes to overcome a filibuster).

Market economy: private firms make most decisions; Congress sets taxes and spending; the Federal Reserve (independent) sets monetary policy; agencies regulate. Industrial policy has returned (CHIPS Act 2022, tariffs).
Expansion of rights by amendment and struggle (13th–15th, 19th, 24th, 26th Amendments; Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts).
Protected by the First Amendment, though with historical exceptions (Alien and Sedition Acts 1798, Palmer Raids, McCarthyism, COINTELPRO).
The world’s largest economy and longest-surviving written constitution. Also gridlock, high cost of campaigns, and recurring fights over executive power.
Supporters say dividing power protects liberty and has lasted 235+ years.
Critics point to the Senate’s and Electoral College’s overrepresentation of small states, the role of money (Citizens United, 2010), gerrymandering, and gridlock.
founded between c. 1142 and c. 1450 (date debated) – today

A league of five, later six, nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and from about 1722 the Tuscarora) united under the Great Law of Peace, traditionally credited to the Peacemaker and Hiawatha. Decisions were made by consensus in a Grand Council, with clan mothers holding the power to choose and remove chiefs.

Distributed. Clan mothers of matrilineal clans nominate and can depose the 50 hereditary chiefs (sachems). Each nation keeps its own affairs; the Grand Council handles shared matters such as war and peace.
They pass it “across the fire” to the Oneida and Cayuga, who deliberate.
Matrilineal clans held land; women controlled agriculture (corn, beans, squash: the “Three Sisters”) and households; men hunted, traded and conducted diplomacy and war. Reciprocity and gift exchange.

Historians debate how much it influenced the US Constitution: Congress recognized an influence in 1988, while many historians (e.g. Tooker, Payne) argue the evidence is thin; Haudenosaunee and other scholars (Johansen, Grinde) argue it was real.

India was ruled from London through a viceroy and a small elite civil service. About 1,000–1,500 British officials of the Indian Civil Service governed hundreds of millions, alongside about 565 princely states ruled by Indian princes under British supervision.
The Secretary of State for India in London and the Viceroy; the Indian Civil Service; the British-officered Indian Army. Indians had very limited representation until reforms in 1909, 1919 and 1935.
Officials appointed by Britain; ICS entry by exams held mainly in London until 1922. Indians were gradually admitted but remained a minority of senior officials until the 1940s.

Very restricted: limited legislative councils (1861, 1909), separate electorates for Muslims (1909), provincial elections with about 10–14% of adults eligible after 1935. Most political participation was through the Indian National Congress, Muslim League, petitions, boycotts and mass civil disobedience.

India paid for its own administration and army, plus “home charges” to Britain; land revenue was the main tax; British goods entered freely while Indian textiles declined; railways and irrigation were built, mainly to serve trade and security.
Official: order, law and “improvement”. In practice: security of the empire, revenue, markets and a large army for imperial wars.
Railways, telegraphs, universities, a unified legal system; also repeated famines and slow per-capita growth (roughly zero between 1900 and 1947 by many estimates).
Sedition laws, press censorship, detention without trial (Rowlatt Act 1919), the Amritsar massacre (1919: 379 killed by official count, more by Indian estimates), mass arrests of Congress leaders.
Indian nationalists (Naoroji, Nehru) and historians (Tharoor, Patnaik, Davis) argue it drained wealth, deindustrialized India, and presided over famines that killed tens of millions.

On paper, a federation of soviet (council) republics run by elected councils of workers, with a constitution guaranteeing rights. In reality, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union (CPSU) controlled every institution under the principle of “democratic centralism”, and the economy was run by central plans.

The Politburo (about 10–15 members) and the General Secretary made the key decisions. The Secretariat controlled appointments through the nomenklatura system. The secret police (Cheka, NKVD, KGB) and the army were party-controlled. Under Stalin, power became personal dictatorship.

Formally, upward elections: party members elect congress delegates, who elect the Central Committee, which elects the Politburo and General Secretary. In practice, leaders chose their successors and lower officials through the nomenklatura; leadership changed through death, intrigue or ouster (Khrushchev, 1964).

Citizens voted in Supreme Soviet and local soviet elections with one approved candidate per seat; official turnout and approval were over 99%. Participation meant joining the party, Komsomol, trade unions (party-controlled), meetings, letters to newspapers and officials. In 1989 Gorbachev allowed competitive elections to a new Congress of People’s Deputies.

Measured by plan fulfillment (tons of steel, coal, grain). Rapid industrialization, mass literacy, universal health care and education, space firsts (Sputnik 1957, Gagarin 1961), victory in WWII, nuclear parity.
Almost none outside the party. Courts and press were party-controlled; the 1936 constitution’s rights were not enforced.

Under Stalin: purges, show trials, the Gulag, executions (about 680,000–750,000 in 1937–38). After 1953: fewer killings; dissidents were jailed, exiled or put in psychiatric hospitals; samizdat circulated secretly.
A superpower, but growth slowed to near zero by the 1980s, chronic shortages and queues, environmental disasters, and collapse in 1991.
Critics cite mass terror, famine, lack of freedom and elections, inefficiency of planning without prices (the “calculation problem”), and economic stagnation.

Mussolini turned a parliamentary monarchy into a one-party dictatorship while keeping the king and the Church. Parliament was replaced by appointed bodies; economic life was organized into “corporations” of employers and workers under state control.

Mussolini as Duce and head of government; the Grand Council of Fascism; the Fascist Party (PNF) and militia (MVSN); the secret police (OVRA). The king, the army and the Church kept some independent power, which is why the king could dismiss Mussolini in July 1943.
Mussolini was appointed by the king in 1922 and never faced a free election again. The Grand Council drew up the national list of candidates.

After 1928, voters could only approve or reject a single national list of 400 candidates (1929 and 1934 plebiscites: about 98–99.8% yes). Participation meant membership in the party, the Opera Nazionale Balilla youth movement, the Dopolavoro leisure organization, rallies and parades.
Approved by the rubber-stamp Chamber (from 1939 the Chamber of Fasces and Corporations).

Corporatism: employers and workers were grouped by sector into state-supervised corporations; strikes were banned; wages set by collective contracts under state control. Private property remained. After 1929 the state rescued banks and created IRI (1933), which came to own a large share of industry. Autarky (self-sufficiency) and the “Battle for Grain”.
Public works, the draining of the Pontine Marshes, the 1929 settlement with the Vatican. But living standards stagnated and real wages fell in the 1920s–30s by most estimates.
Opposition parties and free unions banned (1926); about 5,000 sent to confino (internal exile) and special tribunals; the murder of Matteotti (1924) and the Rosselli brothers (1937).
Wars in Ethiopia and Spain, the racial laws of 1938, alliance with Hitler, invasion, civil war and collapse (1943–45).

Hitler was appointed chancellor in January 1933; the Enabling Act (March 1933) let the government make laws without the Reichstag; after Hindenburg’s death (1934) he merged president and chancellor as Führer, confirmed by plebiscite (about 90% yes).

Single-list Reichstag elections and plebiscites with 90–99% yes votes. Participation meant mass rallies, the Hitler Youth, Winter Relief collections, Strength Through Joy holidays, and block wardens watching neighbors.
Agencies compete to “work towards the Führer” (Ian Kershaw’s phrase).
Courts follow “healthy popular feeling”; special courts and the SS act outside the law.

Capitalist ownership kept (except for Jewish property, which was “Aryanized”), but under heavy state direction: wage and price controls, the Four-Year Plan (1936) for war readiness and autarky, public works, and massive rearmament financed by hidden deficits (Mefo bills). Later plunder of occupied Europe and slave labor.
Racial purity, Lebensraum (living space) in Eastern Europe, the destruction of “Judeo-Bolshevism”, and German world power.
Unemployment fell from about 6 million (1932) to near zero (1938), mostly through rearmament; autobahns; propaganda triumphs (1936 Olympics).
None after 1934. Some resistance (the White Rose, the July 20, 1944 plot) failed.
Concentration camps from 1933 (Dachau), the Night of the Long Knives (1934), the Gestapo, People’s Court executions.
War, the Holocaust, about 6 million Jews murdered, tens of millions of deaths, and the destruction and division of Germany.
Nazi propaganda claimed an economic miracle and national unity; these claims are repeated by neo-Nazis and refuted by historians.
The regime of genocide and aggressive war; historians (Tooze) also show its economy was unsustainable without war and plunder.

When Franco’s coup failed in Barcelona in July 1936, workers led by the anarcho-syndicalist union CNT took over factories, transport and farms. For about a year much of Catalonia and Aragon ran on collectives managed by assemblies, alongside the Republic’s government.
Assemblies and recall; but there was also coercion of reluctant peasants and revolutionary killings of priests and suspected fascists in 1936.
Supporters of the old order faced violence; later the anarchists themselves were suppressed by Communist and Republican forces (May Days 1937).
Ended by the Republic’s recentralization and Franco’s victory in 1939.

A multi-party parliamentary democracy where the Social Democrats governed almost continuously from 1932 to 1976. Its distinctive feature is the bargain between highly organized employers and unions, with the state building a universal welfare state funded by high taxes.
Parliament (Riksdag) and government; but much economic power lies in centralized wage bargaining between the union confederation (LO) and employers (SAF), plus independent government agencies.
Proportional representation (a 4% threshold); governments usually coalitions or minority governments.

Market economy with mostly private firms (Volvo, Ericsson, IKEA), high taxes (tax revenue about 40–50% of GDP), universal welfare, the Rehn–Meidner model (equal pay for equal work across firms, active labor market policy pushing workers from weak to strong firms).
Folkhemmet (“the people’s home”): security, equality and full employment within a market economy.
Proportional parliament, free press, freedom of information (since 1766), ombudsmen, independent courts.
Fully legal; but critics note past policies like forced sterilizations (about 63,000, 1934–1976) and treatment of the Sámi.
A 1990s banking and fiscal crisis led to reforms (lower taxes, pension reform, school vouchers); Sweden remains rich and egalitarian.

Critics on the right point to high taxes and the 1970s–90s slowdown; critics on the left note the model has been diluted since the 1990s; others argue Nordic success rests on high trust and homogeneity that are hard to copy.

Switzerland combines a parliament with frequent national referendums and citizens’ initiatives, a collective seven-member executive, and strong cantons (states). Some cantons still vote by show of hands in open-air assemblies (Landsgemeinde).

Deliberately diffused: a seven-member Federal Council that decides collectively (with a rotating, mostly ceremonial president), the parliament, 26 cantons and the voters themselves, who can overturn laws.
referendum can veto laws (50,000 signatures)
initiative to amend constitution (100,000 signatures)

Parliament by proportional representation (National Council) and by canton (Council of States); the Federal Council elected by parliament, traditionally shared among the four largest parties (the “magic formula”).
Voters decide on about 10–15 national questions a year, plus cantonal and local ones. 50,000 signatures force a referendum on any new law; 100,000 can propose a constitutional amendment.
If 50,000 citizens sign within 100 days, a national vote decides.
The people’s veto, federalism, collegial executive.
Highly stable; but women only got the federal vote in 1971 (and in Appenzell Innerrhoden only in 1990, by court order) because men had to vote to grant it.
Critics note low turnout on many votes, influence of money on campaigns, and majorities that can vote against minority rights (e.g. the 2009 minaret ban).
One-party Leninist state with market economy (since 1978)

The Chinese Communist Party (CCP), about 99 million members, leads the state, the army, the economy and society. Under Mao, policy swung through mass campaigns; under Deng and successors, a more institutional party-state ran a fast-growing market economy; under Xi Jinping (since 2012) power has re-centralized around one leader.

The General Secretary (also state president and head of the Central Military Commission) and the 7-member Politburo Standing Committee; the 24-member Politburo; the Organization Department, which controls appointments; the People’s Liberation Army, which is the party’s army.
Leaders are chosen within the party through consultation, factional bargaining and the Party Congress every five years. Xi abolished presidential term limits in 2018 and began a third term in 2022.

Under Mao: Soviet-style planning and communes. Since 1978: a “socialist market economy”, with private firms producing most output and employment while the state controls banks, land, strategic industries and five-year plans that set priorities (e.g. Made in China 2025). Officials are promoted partly on local growth.
National rejuvenation, prosperity (“moderately prosperous society”), party rule, unification with Taiwan, technological self-reliance.
Measured by GDP growth, poverty reduction, technology and plan targets. About 800 million people left extreme poverty; China became the world’s largest manufacturer.
Censorship (the Great Firewall), the Tiananmen massacre (1989), imprisonment of dissidents (Liu Xiaobo), mass detention in Xinjiang, the National Security Law in Hong Kong (2020).
The fastest sustained growth of a large economy in history, alongside the Great Leap famine, the Cultural Revolution, and extensive repression.
Supporters credit long-term planning, competent cadres and stability (“meritocracy”, Daniel Bell).

After Tito broke with Stalin in 1948, Yugoslavia built a distinctive socialism: firms were “socially owned” and run by elected workers’ councils, prices were partly set by markets, and the country was non-aligned between East and West, while the League of Communists kept a political monopoly.
Tito personally (president for life from 1974), the League of Communists, the army and security police; later the six republics and two provinces gained power, especially after the 1974 constitution.
Party-controlled appointments; after Tito’s death (1980) a rotating collective presidency.
Market socialism: competing self-managed firms, Western loans, tourism, guest workers abroad (about 1 million in Western Europe by the 1970s).
Fast growth in the 1950s–70s; Yugoslavs could travel abroad freely.
Goli Otok prison camp for Stalinists (1949–56); dissidents such as Milovan Djilas jailed.
Debt crisis and inflation in the 1980s, then nationalist breakup and wars (1991–2001).
Cuba is ruled by the Communist Party of Cuba, which the constitution defines as the leading force of society. The economy is mostly state-run, with growing private small businesses since 2021.
The party’s Political Bureau and First Secretary (Fidel Castro to 2011, Raúl Castro to 2021, Miguel Díaz-Canel since); the army, which also runs much of the economy (GAESA).

Local municipal elections have multiple candidates (no party campaigning); national lists are single-slate. Mass organizations (CDR, unions, women’s federation) mobilize participation; a 2018–19 constitutional consultation and a 2022 referendum on the family code.
Central planning; ration book (libreta) since 1962; dependence first on Soviet subsidies, later on Venezuela, tourism and remittances; small private businesses legalized in 2021.
Literacy campaign (1961), life expectancy similar to the US, many doctors per person; economic stagnation, shortages and blackouts.
Political prisoners; after the July 11, 2021 protests, hundreds were sentenced; emigration of over 10% of the population since 2021.

A hybrid: an elected president and parliament, but supreme authority belongs to an Islamic jurist, the Supreme Leader, under Khomeini’s doctrine of velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist). Unelected councils vet candidates and laws. (After Khamenei was killed in 2026, succession is a developing story.)
Competitive but restricted elections; turnout has fallen (about 41% in the 2024 parliamentary election, a record low).
Mass executions (1988), crackdowns on the Green Movement (2009) and the “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests (2022, hundreds killed).
Critics see an authoritarian theocracy with fake competition.

The People’s Action Party (PAP) has won every election since 1959. Elections are real and clean at the ballot box, but the rules (group constituencies, defamation suits, media control) make opposition very hard. Government emphasizes merit, planning and pragmatism.
Housing Board (~80% live in public housing)
Detention without trial historically (Operation Coldstore 1963); defamation suits against opposition.

Twenty-seven countries pool sovereignty in some areas (trade, single market, competition, and for 20 members the euro), with shared institutions that make binding law, while keeping national control over defense, most taxes and foreign policy.
European Parliament elections (proportional); European Citizens’ Initiative (1 million signatures); national elections choose the governments in the councils.
Parliament and the Council each amend and adopt (qualified majority in Council: 55% of states, 65% of population).
Peace in Europe, prosperity, “ever closer union”, democracy and rule of law.
No war among members since its founding; a single market of about 450 million people.
Legal; Euroskeptic parties sit in Parliament; Britain left (2020).
Critics cite a “democratic deficit”, bureaucracy, loss of national sovereignty and one-size-fits-all monetary policy.
Elections with excluded opponents (Navalny barred, imprisoned, died in prison 2024); 2020 amendments let Putin potentially rule to 2036.
Managed elections; protest heavily restricted, especially since 2022.
Market economy dominated by state and loyal private conglomerates, energy exports; since 2022 a war economy.
Recovery from the 1990s collapse in the 2000s; stagnation since 2014.
Journalists and opponents killed or jailed; “foreign agent” laws.
Supporters credit Putin with restoring order and national pride after the chaotic 1990s.
Critics describe a kleptocratic dictatorship that started the largest war in Europe since 1945.

A Westminster-style parliamentary democracy with a written constitution (drafted under B. R. Ambedkar), a federal system of 28 states, an independent Election Commission and Supreme Court. Nearly a billion people are eligible to vote.
Prime minister and cabinet with a Lok Sabha majority; state governments; the Supreme Court; powerful parties (Congress dominant until 1989; BJP since 2014).
National elections over several weeks with electronic voting machines; turnout about 66%; village councils give local participation.
Supreme Court may review under the “basic structure” doctrine.
Planned mixed economy (Five-Year Plans, Planning Commission) until 1991 reforms; now a market economy with large public sector.
Survived as a democracy (except the 1975–77 Emergency); rapid growth since the 1990s.
Legal, but V-Dem and Freedom House report declines in press freedom and civil liberties since about 2014.

After the 1973 coup, a junta of the four armed-service chiefs ruled, with Pinochet soon dominant. Congress was closed, parties banned, and the economy handed to free-market economists (the “Chicago Boys”).
Seizure of power; 1980 constitution approved in a plebiscite under dictatorship.
None until the 1988 plebiscite, which Pinochet lost (56% No).
Privatization, trade opening, private pension system (1981), deregulation.
Inflation tamed, growth after the 1982 crash.
About 3,200 killed or disappeared, about 38,000 tortured (official commissions).

Before 1492 the Americas held perhaps 40–60 million people (estimates range from 8 to over 100 million) in hundreds of nations: cities larger than any in Europe, confederacies with written constitutions in oral form, empires with road networks, and small bands of hunters. Similar worlds existed in Australia, New Zealand, the Pacific, Siberia, the Arctic and Africa. This section follows what happen
Perhaps 10,000–20,000 at its peak, the largest city north of Mexico
Planned plazas, mound platforms, a solar calendar of wooden posts (“Woodhenge”).
Six nations bound by the Great Law of Peace; a Grand Council of 50 chiefs nominated and removable by clan mothers; decisions by consensus (see How systems work).
Played Britain and France against each other for a century; split during the American Revolution; much land lost in the Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1784) and later.
Tenochtitlan perhaps 200,000; the empire several million
A Triple Alliance of city-states; the tlatoani (“speaker”) was elected by a council of nobles from the royal family; about 400 tributary towns paid goods to the capital.
Schools for all boys, ritual human sacrifice, a 365-day calendar.
Cortés allied with the Tlaxcalans and other enemies of the Mexica; a smallpox epidemic in 1520 killed a large share of the city; Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521.
The Sapa Inca, believed descended from the Sun, ruled through four provinces and a decimal administration (units of 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 households).

No markets or money in the core economy: households owed labor (mit’a) to the state, which stored food and cloth in thousands of warehouses and redistributed them. About 40,000 km of roads. Records kept on knotted cords (quipu).
Weakened by smallpox and a civil war; Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532; resistance continued until 1572. Túpac Amaru II led a huge revolt in 1780–81.
Classic period c. 250–900; independent states until 1697
The only fully developed writing system of the pre-Columbian Americas, a base-20 number system with zero, precise astronomy and calendars.
Spanish conquest took nearly two centuries; the last independent Maya kingdom (Nojpetén) fell in 1697. Bishop Landa burned Maya books in 1562; only four codices survive.
About 6 million Maya people; Guatemala’s Maya majority suffered genocide in 1981–83.
Multi-story adobe towns (Acoma has been inhabited for about 800 years).
In the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, led by Popé, the Pueblos expelled the Spanish for 12 years, one of the most successful Indigenous revolts in North America.
19 Pueblos in New Mexico plus the Hopi in Arizona.
Town councils and a women’s council; adopted a written constitution with three branches in 1827.
Sequoyah created a syllabary (1821) and most Cherokee became literate within a few years; the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper began in 1828.
Won Worcester v. Georgia (1832) in the Supreme Court, but were forcibly removed in 1838 on the Trail of Tears.
The largest US tribe (Cherokee Nation about 450,000 citizens).
Ancient; Plains horse culture from the 1700s
Perhaps 15,000–20,000 Lakota in the mid-1800s

Won Red Cloud’s War and the Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) guaranteeing the Black Hills; the US seized them after gold was found; defeated Custer at Little Bighorn (1876); massacred at Wounded Knee (1890).
In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the Black Hills were taken illegally; the Lakota refused the money, now over $2 billion, and still demand the land.
Historian Pekka Hämäläinen argues they ran a regional empire that dominated Spanish and Mexican frontier societies; defeated by the US Army and the destruction of the bison by 1875.
Smallpox in 1862 killed perhaps half the population of the BC coast. Canada banned the potlatch from 1884 to 1951.
Haida, Tlingit, Kwakwaka’wakw, Coast Salish and others; major treaty and title cases (Delgamuukw 1997, Tsilhqot’in 2014).
Estimates for Hispaniola range from about 100,000 to several million in 1492
Resisted the Inca and then Spain for over 300 years; Spain recognized a frontier by treaty (Quillín, 1641).
Conquered by Chile (1861–1883) and Argentina (1878–1885).
About 1.7 million in Chile; ongoing land conflicts and a rejected 2022 constitution that would have recognized Indigenous nations.
Estimates for 1788 range from about 300,000 to over 1 million
The oldest continuous cultures on Earth; about 250 languages.
Britain claimed Australia as terra nullius (“nobody’s land”) in 1788. Frontier wars and massacres, disease and dispossession followed.
About 3.8% of Australians; the 1992 Mabo decision overturned terra nullius; the 2023 Voice referendum failed (about 60% No).
The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) was signed in English and Māori versions that differ on sovereignty; wars and land confiscations followed (1845–1872).
About 17% of New Zealanders; Waitangi Tribunal (1975) and treaty settlements; Māori seats in Parliament since 1867.
About 300,000 or more in 1778 (estimates up to 800,000)
Chiefdoms unified by Kamehameha I (1810) into a kingdom; a constitutional monarchy from 1840.
A highly literate kingdom in the 1800s with Hawaiian-language newspapers.
Disease reduced the population to about 40,000 by the 1890s. American businessmen overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893 with US Marines landed; the US annexed Hawaiʻi in 1898.
The US Congress apologized for the overthrow in 1993.
Siida (herding communities); today elected Sámi parliaments (Norway 1989, Sweden 1993, Finland 1996).
Forced assimilation (Norwegianization), boarding schools, and Sweden’s State Institute for Racial Biology (1922) measured Sámi skulls.
Land rights disputes over mines and wind farms (Fosen ruling, 2021).
Japan annexed Hokkaido in 1869 and banned Ainu customs and language under assimilation laws (1899 Former Natives Protection Act).
Japan recognized the Ainu as Indigenous only in 2019.

Papal bulls (1452, 1493) and later law claimed that Christian nations “discovering” lands gained rights over them. US Chief Justice Marshall wrote it into American law in Johnson v. M’Intosh (1823). The Vatican formally repudiated the doctrine in 2023.
“Nobody’s land”: the legal fiction that Australia and other places belonged to no one. Overturned in Australia by the High Court in Mabo (1992).

A form of colonialism where settlers come to stay and replace the Indigenous population on the land, rather than mainly extracting labor (Patrick Wolfe: “invasion is a structure, not an event”). Critics say the concept can flatten very different histories.

The US made about 370 ratified treaties with Native nations (1778–1871), recognizing them as nations. Most were broken or renegotiated under pressure, but they remain law and are enforced in modern court cases (McGirt v. Oklahoma, 2020).
In US law, tribes are “domestic dependent nations” (Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, 1831) with their own governments, courts and laws, subject to Congress. About 574 federally recognized tribes today.
Land set aside for Native nations, often far smaller than their territories. About 56 million acres in the US today are held in trust.
US rules measuring Native identity by fraction of ancestry, introduced by the federal government; many tribes now use lineal descent instead. Critics call it “statistical extermination”.

The 1948 UN Convention defines genocide as acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial or religious group: killing, serious harm, conditions of life calculated to destroy, preventing births, or forcibly transferring children. Raphael Lemkin, who coined the word, studied colonial cases including the Americas.

The UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (2007), adopted 143–4; the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand voted against and later endorsed it. It affirms self-determination and “free, prior and informed consent”.
How many people lived in the Americas in 1492?

Estimates range from about 8 million (Kroeber, 1939) to over 100 million (Dobyns, 1966). Many scholars today accept roughly 40–60 million for the hemisphere (Denevan: 54 million) and 2–7 million north of Mexico. Low estimates once suited claims of an “empty” continent.

Most deaths came from Old World diseases (smallpox, measles, influenza) to which Native people had no immunity. But historians (Reséndez, Jones, Cameron) show that enslavement, war, forced labor, displacement and famine made epidemics far deadlier and prevented recovery. It is not “either/or”.

Scholars agree specific episodes meet the UN definition (California 1846–73 per Madley; the Guatemalan Maya genocide per a UN commission; Herero and Nama). Whether colonization as a whole was genocide is debated: Ostler, Dunbar-Ortiz and Stannard say yes; others (Anderson prefers “ethnic cleansing”; Lewy argued most deaths lacked genocidal intent). At Fort Pitt (1763), British officers gave blankets from a smallpox hospital to Delaware envoys, with documented intent; whether it caused an outbreak is unknown. Stories of widespread deliberate infection (e.g. the 1837 Mandan epidemic) are not supported by evidence.
Franklin admired the Confederacy and Congress acknowledged an influence in 1988; many historians find little direct evidence in the Constitution’s drafting.
Neither stereotype fits. Societies ranged from democratic confederacies to empires with slavery and human sacrifice, as everywhere. Both “noble savage” and “savage” myths served colonial politics.

After Britain defeated France, an alliance of nations led by the Odawa leader Pontiac captured eight British forts. Britain issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763, reserving land west of the Appalachians for Native nations.

A Western Confederacy of nations defeated two US armies, including St. Clair’s defeat (1791), the worst defeat of the US Army by Native forces, before losing at Fallen Timbers (1794). Later the Shawnee leader Tecumseh and his brother the Prophet built a pan-Indian alliance that fought alongside Britain in the War of 1812; Tecumseh was killed in 1813.
The Treaty of Greenville (1795) ceded most of Ohio. Tecumseh’s death ended the last great attempt at a united Native resistance east of the Mississippi.
Americans saw westward expansion as spreading liberty and farms; the Northwest Ordinance (1787) promised “utmost good faith” toward Indians.
St. Clair lost about 600–900 soldiers in 1791.

President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act (1830). The Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw, about 60,000 people, were forced west of the Mississippi. The Cherokee won in the Supreme Court (Worcester v. Georgia, 1832), but the government ignored the ruling.

Southern states and settlers wanted cotton land and gold (found in Cherokee country in 1828); Jacksonian democracy rested on land for white farmers; racial ideas that Native people could not live alongside whites.
About 4,000 of roughly 16,000 Cherokee died on the Trail of Tears (1838–39), by commonly cited estimates; similar losses struck other nations. The Seminole fought three wars rather than leave.
A failure of the rule of law: the courts upheld Cherokee rights and the executive defied them.
The model of ethnic cleansing later studied by other settler states.
The Supreme Court ruled for the Cherokee in Worcester v. Georgia (1832).
Many historians call removal ethnic cleansing; others argue the foreseeable mass death meets the genocide definition.

After the US conquest and the Gold Rush, militias, vigilantes and the US Army killed thousands of California Indians; state laws allowed Native people, including children, to be forced into servitude. The state reimbursed militia campaigns, and the federal government repaid the state.
Gold and land; settler demands to remove Native people; racial ideology; state and federal funding of killing campaigns.
California’s Native population, perhaps 150,000 in 1846, had already fallen sharply under Spanish missions.

The Native population fell to about 30,000 by 1873. Historian Benjamin Madley documents 9,492–16,094 killings; disease, starvation and servitude killed many more. Governor Peter Burnett said in 1851 that a “war of extermination” would continue until the race became extinct.
Recognized by California’s governor in 2019, who formally apologized and called it genocide.
A case where democracy (settler voters and their elected officials) directly funded mass killing.
A clear case of genocide under the UN definition, according to Madley’s An American Genocide (2016).
California’s 1850 Act for the Government and Protection of Indians allowed forced indenture.
Governor Newsom formally apologized in 2019.
Does it meet the legal definition of genocide?

After the Dakota War (1862), 38 Dakota men were hanged in Mankato, the largest mass execution in US history. At Sand Creek (1864) Colorado volunteers massacred about 150–230 Cheyenne and Arapaho, mostly women, children and the elderly, under a US flag. The Navajo were marched to Bosque Redondo (the Long Walk, 1864). The Lakota and allies defeated Custer at Little Bighorn (1876). The US Army killed
Railroads, gold (the Black Hills), settlers under the Homestead Act (1862), and a policy of confining nations to reservations.
The bison, the Plains nations’ economy, were slaughtered by commercial hunters from tens of millions to under 1,000 by 1889, with army encouragement.
By 1890 the Plains nations were confined to reservations; the census declared the frontier closed.
Reformers of the time (Helen Hunt Jackson, A Century of Dishonor, 1881) condemned broken treaties but promoted assimilation as the alternative.
Generals like Sherman and Sheridan framed it as necessary to secure the West; military honors were given for Wounded Knee (20 Medals of Honor, still not rescinded).
Part of the global wave of settler conquest in the 1870s–90s.
Sand Creek was investigated by Congress in 1865 and condemned as a massacre.
The bison population collapsed to near extinction by 1889.
Officers praised it as starving the Plains nations; historians debate how much was policy versus market demand.
Allotment and boarding schools: “Kill the Indian, save the man”

The Dawes Act (1887) broke up communal reservations into individual plots and sold the “surplus” to settlers. Boarding schools, starting with Carlisle (1879), removed children from their families to erase their languages and cultures; Carlisle’s founder Richard Pratt’s motto was to “kill the Indian in him, and save the man”. Canada ran a parallel residential school system (1880s–1996).
Reformers believed assimilation into private farming and Christianity would “civilize” Native people; settlers wanted the land.

Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres (1887) to about 48 million (1934). A US Interior Department investigation (2022–24) identified 417 federal boarding schools and at least 973 children who died in them. Canada’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015) documented over 3,200 deaths (later records raise it above 4,000) among about 150,000 children.
Christian missions ran most schools; churches have since apologized (Pope Francis in Canada, 2022).
The US Interior Department documented 417 federal schools and at least 973 deaths.
President Biden formally apologized for the boarding schools in October 2024.
The UN definition includes forcibly transferring children of a group to another group. Canada’s TRC called it cultural genocide; Canada’s Parliament later called it genocide.
Ground-penetrating radar has found many possible burial sites (e.g. Kamloops 2021); most have not been excavated.

British colonization proceeded on the claim of terra nullius. Frontier conflict lasted from the 1790s to the 1920s; researchers at the University of Newcastle have mapped over 400 massacres. In Tasmania, the “Black War” (1820s–1832) and removal to Flinders Island nearly destroyed the Aboriginal population.
Disease (smallpox in 1789) killed many before settlers arrived in some regions.

The Aboriginal population fell to perhaps under 100,000 by the early 1900s. In 1838, settlers were hanged for the Myall Creek massacre, a rare prosecution; the Coniston massacre (1928) was officially ruled justified.
In Australia’s “history wars” (Keith Windschuttle, 2002) some conservatives disputed the scale of massacres.
Terra nullius was rejected by Australia’s High Court in 1992.

In 1840 about 500 Māori chiefs and the British Crown signed the Treaty of Waitangi. The English version ceded “sovereignty”; the Māori version granted “kāwanatanga” (governorship) while guaranteeing “tino rangatiratanga” (full chieftainship). Wars followed over land, with large confiscations (raupatu).
About 3,000 deaths in the wars; millions of acres confiscated or purchased under pressure; the Māori population fell to about 42,000 by 1896.
Māori see the treaty as a partnership the Crown broke; the Kīngitanga (King Movement, 1858) united tribes to protect land.
The treaty is now treated as New Zealand’s founding document; the Waitangi Tribunal (1975) investigates breaches.

Some New Zealand conservatives and libertarians (the 2024 Treaty Principles Bill) argue the treaty should mean equal rights for all, not special rights; tens of thousands marched against it, and Parliament defeated the bill in 2025.
The Waitangi Tribunal (2014) found the signatories did not cede sovereignty.

After decades of war, the Russian Empire completed its conquest of the Circassians in 1864 and expelled most of the survivors to the Ottoman Empire. Many died in the mountains, on the coast and in overcrowded ships and camps.
Winter expulsions, epidemics, starvation.
Estimates of deaths range from hundreds of thousands upward; about 90% of Circassians ended up outside their homeland. Georgia recognized it as genocide in 2011; Russia does not.
Circassians worldwide commemorate May 21 as a day of mourning.
Most Circassians were expelled from their homeland in 1864.

American and European businessmen, backed by US Marines, overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani in 1893. President Cleveland called it an act of war and asked for her restoration, but the US annexed Hawaiʻi in 1898 despite petitions signed by most Native Hawaiians.
Sugar planters wanted duty-free access to US markets; the Queen tried to restore royal power and Native voting rights curtailed by the 1887 “Bayonet Constitution”.
Disease had reduced Native Hawaiians from hundreds of thousands to about 40,000.
A US territory (1898), then state (1959). In 1993 Congress formally apologized.
The 1993 Apology Resolution acknowledged the overthrow was illegal and involved US agents.

Argentina’s army conquered Patagonia (the “Conquest of the Desert”, 1878–85), killing and capturing thousands of Mapuche, Tehuelche and others; Chile occupied Araucanía (1861–83). In the Putumayo rubber zone (1879–1912), the Peruvian Amazon Company enslaved and killed Indigenous workers. Mexico deported thousands of Yaqui to plantations in Yucatán (1900s).
Roger Casement’s 1912 report estimated about 30,000 deaths in the Putumayo. In Argentina, captured people were distributed as servants.
Casement’s report documented torture and killings in the Putumayo.
Australia (also Canada’s “Sixties Scoop”)

Australian governments and churches removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, especially of mixed descent, from their families to be raised in institutions or white families. Canada’s “Sixties Scoop” placed thousands of Indigenous children with non-Indigenous families.
Assimilation policy and the belief that Aboriginal people would “die out” and mixed-descent children could be absorbed.
The 1997 Bringing Them Home report estimated that between one in three and one in ten Indigenous children were removed from 1910 to 1970. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologized in 2008.
The report concluded that forcible removal met the definition of genocide.
Some conservative critics (e.g. in the “history wars”) argued many removals were for welfare.
The national apology was delivered in 2008.

Native Americans became US citizens in 1924, though some states blocked voting into the 1950s. In the 1950s the US tried to end (“terminate”) tribes and relocate people to cities. Activists responded: the occupation of Alcatraz (1969–71), the American Indian Movement (AIM), the Trail of Broken Treaties (1972) and the 71-day standoff at Wounded Knee (1973).
Deep poverty on reservations; a 1976 government report found the Indian Health Service had sterilized thousands of Native women, many without informed consent.
President Nixon renounced termination (1970). The Indian Self-Determination Act (1975), the Indian Child Welfare Act (1978) and the American Indian Religious Freedom Act (1978) followed.
The turn from survival to resurgence and self-determination; Vine Deloria Jr.’s Custer Died for Your Sins (1969) reshaped debate.
A 1976 GAO report documented 3,406 sterilizations in four IHS areas over three years.
The Guatemalan civil war and the Maya genocide
In a 36-year civil war, the US-backed military fought leftist guerrillas. Under General Efraín Ríos Montt (1982–83) the army destroyed over 600 Maya villages in a scorched-earth campaign.
The 1954 US-backed coup, land inequality, Cold War anti-communism, and racism against the Maya majority.

About 200,000 killed or disappeared, over 80% of them Maya. The UN-backed truth commission (1999) found the state committed acts of genocide. Ríos Montt was convicted of genocide in 2013 (overturned on procedure; he died during retrial).
Rigoberta Menchú, a K’iche’ Maya survivor, won the Nobel Peace Prize (1992).
President Clinton apologized in 1999 for US support for the Guatemalan military.
The UN commission attributed 93% of violations to state forces.

Indigenous nations won major legal and political victories: Australia’s Mabo decision (1992), Nunavut (1999), UNDRIP (2007), Canada’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (2015), Standing Rock protests against the Dakota Access Pipeline (2016), McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020, much of eastern Oklahoma remains reservation land), Deb Haaland as the first Native US cabinet secretary (2021), the Supreme Court
Some conservatives object to separate rights or jurisdiction (e.g. the dissent in McGirt and the 2023 Voice No campaign); Justice Gorsuch, a conservative, wrote McGirt on originalist grounds.
McGirt (2020) held that the Muscogee reservation was never disestablished.
Euler founded graph theory (the Königsberg bridges, 1736), standardized notation (e, i, f(x), π) and advanced calculus, mechanics and number theory.
He also divided humans into “varieties” with character traits, an early step toward scientific racism used to justify slavery and colonialism.
Argued that the division of labor and free exchange, guided by the “invisible hand”, create national wealth.
Lavoisier was a tax farmer for the old regime and was guillotined in 1794; the judge supposedly said “the Republic has no need of scientists”.
In “What is Enlightenment?” (1784) and his critiques, Kant argued for autonomy of reason; in Perpetual Peace (1795) he imagined a federation of republics.
The first vaccine; smallpox killed perhaps 300 million people in the 20th century alone before its eradication.
Napoleon had his army vaccinated; Spain’s Balmis expedition (1803) carried vaccine to its colonies using orphan boys as living carriers. Smallpox had devastated Indigenous peoples since 1492.
Used to oppose poor relief and to excuse famine policy in Ireland and India; the Industrial Revolution and Green Revolution broke his trap.
Romantic nationalism (Herder, Fichte) fed the national movements of 1848 and, in distorted forms, later ethno-nationalism. Goya’s Third of May 1808 painted the horror of Napoleonic war.
History as the unfolding of reason and freedom through conflict (thesis, antithesis, synthesis is a simplification); “the truth is the whole”.
Left Hegelians (Marx) and Right Hegelians split over whether the Prussian state was history’s goal; Fukuyama’s “end of history” is Hegelian.
Electrification in the Second Industrial Revolution; Lenin later said communism was “Soviet power plus the electrification of the whole country”.
Babbage also wrote On the Economy of Machinery (1832), which Marx used to analyze factory labor.
Instant long-distance communication; transatlantic cable (1866).
Enabled global markets, news agencies, imperial command (India), railways and the 1873 panic’s rapid spread.
Snow traced a London cholera outbreak to a water pump using a map; Nightingale used statistics (her rose diagram) to show soldiers died more from disease than wounds.
Public sanitation (London’s sewers, 1860s) did more for life expectancy than any medicine of the century: a case for state action that liberals and socialists both claimed.
Misused as “Social Darwinism” (Spencer) to justify laissez-faire, racism and imperialism, and later eugenics and Nazi racial ideology; Marx admired the book; Kropotkin answered with Mutual Aid.
The theory behind social democratic and communist parties, the Russian and Chinese revolutions, and much of 20th-century social science.
Radio and later radar transformed war and mass politics (Roosevelt’s fireside chats, Goebbels’ “people’s receiver”).
The first commercial power stations and the AC vs DC “war of the currents”.
Changed how the 20th century understood the self.
His nephew Edward Bernays turned crowd psychology into modern public relations and propaganda.
Modernism split politically: Futurists celebrated war and joined fascism; Soviet avant-gardists were later crushed by socialist realism; the Nazis banned “degenerate art” (1937).
First powered flight (1903); Ford’s moving assembly line (1913) made the Model T affordable.
“Fordism” (high wages, mass production) became a model for the postwar economy; airplanes turned cities into targets in WWII.
Special relativity (1905) and general relativity (1915) replaced Newton’s absolute space and time; mass and energy are equivalent.
The Nazis attacked “Jewish physics”; Einstein fled in 1933 and his 1939 letter to Roosevelt helped start the Manhattan Project.
Also made explosives for Germany in WWI; Haber personally led chlorine gas attacks (1915), and his institute developed the pesticide later adapted as Zyklon B.
The intellectual basis of the postwar Golden Age and of stimulus in 2008 and 2020; attacked by Hayek and Friedman.
Discovered 1928; mass-produced during WWII.
Made bacterial infections curable; saved perhaps 200 million lives.
Defined computation mathematically (1936); led the breaking of the German Enigma cipher at Bletchley Park.
Codebreaking shortened WWII; Britain later prosecuted Turing for homosexuality (1952); he died in 1954 and was pardoned in 2013.
A movement to “improve” human heredity by controlling reproduction.
Mainstream science in the early 1900s across the political spectrum, later discredited.
About 60,000 forced sterilizations in the US; Sweden about 63,000; Nazi Germany sterilized about 400,000 and then murdered disabled people (Aktion T4) as a step toward the Holocaust.
Oppenheimer, Fermi, Szilard and about 130,000 workers
Hiroshima and Nagasaki; the arms race; the uranium mining and testing that harmed Navajo and Marshall Islanders; Soviet spies sped up the Soviet bomb (1949).
ENIAC team, von Neumann; Bardeen, Brattain, Shockley (transistor 1947)
Claude Shannon; John von Neumann & Oskar Morgenstern (1944); John Nash
Franklin’s data was used without her knowledge; she died in 1958 before the Nobel Prize (1962).
Doubled grain yields in Asia; credited with saving hundreds of millions from famine.
Sputnik (1957), Gagarin (1961), Apollo 11 Moon landing (1969).
A Cold War contest for prestige; von Braun had built V-2 rockets for the Nazis with concentration-camp labor before working for the US.
Led to the EPA (1970) under Nixon; environmental politics later became central to left and right divides.
Alfred Wegener (1912), Marie Tharp, Harry Hess, others
Tharp’s seafloor maps (1950s) came partly from Cold War submarine research.
ARPA, Vint Cerf & Bob Kahn (TCP/IP), Tim Berners-Lee (Web, 1989)
Enabled globalized supply chains, the Arab Spring, social-media populism and mass surveillance (Snowden, 2013).
Famines are caused by loss of entitlements (people’s ability to buy or grow food), not just lack of food; no major famine has occurred in a functioning democracy with a free press.
Cures for genetic diseases (first approved 2023).
Raised ethical alarms when a Chinese scientist edited human embryos (2018).

NASA’s New Horizons flew past on 14 July 2015 after a 9.5-year trip. The bright “heart” is a plain of frozen nitrogen. In 2006 astronomers reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet because it hasn’t cleared its orbit of other objects.

Io is the most volcanic place known. Jupiter’s gravity squeezes and flexes it every orbit, heating the inside. Scientists predicted this in 1979, and days later Voyager 1 photographed an erupting plume.
Under an ice shell, Europa likely hides a salty ocean with about twice as much water as all of Earth’s oceans. NASA’s Europa Clipper launched in 2024 and is due to arrive in 2030.

This globe is plain orange on purpose. Titan has a thick nitrogen atmosphere (1.5× Earth’s surface pressure) full of orange haze that hides the ground. Under it are lakes of liquid methane. ESA’s Huygens probe landed there in 2005.
In 2005 the Cassini probe found geysers of water spraying from cracks near the south pole, fed by an ocean under the ice. Cassini later flew through the spray and tasted it.
Herschel crater is about 130 km wide, a third of the moon’s own width. The impact that made it nearly shattered Mimas.
Two-faced: one side is dark as coal, the other bright as snow. In 1671 Giovanni Cassini noticed he could see it only on one side of Saturn, and guessed correctly that its two halves differ.

The black areas are not shadows. They were never photographed. Voyager 2, the only visitor (1986), arrived when Uranus’s south pole faced the Sun, so it saw only the southern halves of the moons. Miranda has cliffs about 20 km tall.
A bootprint on the Moon, Apollo 11 (July 1969)
The dark patches are “maria” (seas): old floods of lava that cooled into basalt. The bright areas are older, cratered highlands.
You can never see this side from Earth, because the Moon is tidally locked and always shows us the same face. The Soviet probe Luna 3 photographed it first, in 1959.

A long valley on the Moon, named after a nearby crater, which honors Hypatia of Alexandria, a mathematician killed in 415 CE. Rilles are thought to be collapsed lava channels or places where the crust pulled apart.
Low sun angles throw long shadows, which is how scientists measured the heights of lunar mountains, the same trick Galileo used with his telescope in 1609.

From a small underground party to the world’s second-largest economy: thirteen eras, each one shaped by the last. The same party led the revolution, the deadliest famine in history, the Cultural Revolution, and the largest fall in poverty ever recorded.

Thirteen delegates founded the Communist Party in Shanghai in 1921, with Soviet advice. It allied with Sun Yat-sen’s Nationalists (KMT) to unify a China split among warlords. In April 1927 the Nationalist leader Chiang Kai-shek turned on the communists and massacred thousands in Shanghai.
China had been humiliated by foreign powers for 80 years and was ruled by rival warlords; young radicals looked to the Russian Revolution for a way out.

In Jiangxi, Mao and Zhu De built a peasant army and gave landlords’ land to poor farmers. The party also purged its own ranks: in the Futian incident of 1930–31, thousands of supposed traitors were tortured and killed. Chiang’s armies encircled the base five times.
The defeat of 1927 left the party only the villages, where most Chinese lived.

About 86,000 people broke out of Jiangxi in October 1934. After the Xiang River battle that December, about 30,000 remained, and only roughly 7,000–8,000 reached northern Shaanxi a year later; most losses came from desertion, hunger and disease as well as battle. At Zunyi in January 1935 Mao rose to leadership. Mao gave the distance as 12,500 km; two British researchers who walked the route in 200
The march became the party’s founding legend, and its survivors, the “Long March generation”, ruled China for half a century. Many were later destroyed in the Cultural Revolution.

Japan’s full invasion in 1937 forced a second alliance with the Nationalists. From its base at Yan’an the party grew from tens of thousands to over a million members. The Rectification Movement of 1942–44 made Mao’s thought the party line and forced confessions from suspected spies. Estimates of Chinese deaths in the war run from about 14 to 20 million.

The civil war resumed in 1946. The US backed the Nationalists; the Soviets helped the communists in Manchuria. Hyperinflation, corruption and land reform promises swung peasants and many city people to the communists. Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic on 1 October 1949; Chiang fled to Taiwan.

Landlords were tried before village crowds and many were killed; a campaign against “counter-revolutionaries” followed. Mao himself later said about 700,000 had been killed; historians estimate one to two million deaths in these campaigns. In October 1950 China entered the Korean War against the US; hundreds of thousands of Chinese soldiers died, including Mao’s son. The US imposed a trade embargo

Mao invited criticism of the party in 1956–57. When it came, he reversed course: officially 552,877 people were labelled “rightists”, and estimates of those persecuted run from one to two million. Many were sent to labour camps; at Jiabiangou in Gansu, about 2,500 of some 3,000 prisoners died.
Mao was shaken by the 1956 uprising in Hungary and by Khrushchev’s attack on Stalin.

Communes, backyard steel and inflated harvests led to the deadliest famine in history, 15 to 45 million excess deaths. Critics were purged at Lushan in 1959. In 1962 Liu Shaoqi called it 70% man-made.

Liu and Deng allowed private plots and household farming in places, and the economy recovered. Mao insisted in September 1962 that class struggle must never be forgotten. China tested its first atomic bomb in October 1964.
The famine had discredited Mao’s methods but not his authority.

Mao turned students against the party; the army then restored order with mass purges. 1.1 to 1.6 million died and 22 to 30 million were persecuted. Liu Shaoqi died in detention; Deng was purged twice. Nixon’s visit in 1972 began a new relationship with the US.
Mao feared the party had become “revisionist” and wanted his revolution and power back.
Mao died in September 1976 and his closest allies, the Gang of Four, were arrested within a month.

Deng Xiaoping rehabilitated millions and let farmers farm their own plots, starting with a secret pact by farmers in Xiaogang village in 1978. Special economic zones such as Shenzhen opened to foreign investment; the one-child policy began. Democracy activists such as Wei Jingsheng were jailed. In 1989 protests for reform were crushed by the army.

Deng’s 1992 southern tour restarted reform. China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001 and became the factory of the world; Hong Kong returned in 1997. The World Bank counts about 800 million people lifted out of extreme poverty since 1980. Inequality, pollution and corruption grew with the economy.
After 1989 the party staked its legitimacy on growth.

An anti-corruption campaign removed many officials and rivals. Mass detention in Xinjiang from 2017; a national security law for Hong Kong in 2020; presidential term limits removed in 2018. China declared extreme poverty eliminated by its own measure in 2021 and built the world’s largest high-speed rail network.

Futian (1930), Yan’an (1942–44), the early 1950s, the Anti-Rightist Campaign (1957), the Cultural Revolution and Xinjiang (2017–) all targeted enemies said to be hiding inside. Each campaign taught people that reporting bad news was dangerous.
Warlords, invasion and civil war, then the Cultural Revolution, left Deng’s generation fearing disorder above all. That fear explains 1989, and the stress on stability since.
False harvest reports made the famine worse; the famine was hidden; Tiananmen is erased. Yet China’s own statistics, published in 1983, are among the strongest proof of the famine.
The same party presided over the deadliest famine in history and the largest fall in extreme poverty ever recorded. Both are true, and both belong in the story.
