History is often told from the top: kings, presidents, generals, companies. This deep dive starts from the bottom, with the people whose lives were taken, owned, stolen, starved, poisoned, experimented on or erased. Their experiences are part of the record of every system on this site: empires and republics, capitalist and communist states, fascist regimes, corporations and intelligence agencies.

Many of these harms lasted for generations: slavery, the removal of Indigenous children, land seizures and famine shaped families long after the events ended. Historians, survivors’ descendants and governments still argue about apologies and reparations. Those are real debates. Whether the events happened is not.
A note for readers: these are true stories of great cruelty. They are told factually and without images of the dead. Pictures of violence are blurred until you tap them and hidden for ages 10–12.
Death tolls are estimates with ranges. A range never means doubt about the crime.
Ask who ordered, who profited, who carried out and who looked away.
People were never only victims: they resisted, escaped, hid others, recorded the truth and demanded justice.

About 12.5 million Africans were forced onto slave ships; about 10.7 million survived the crossing. In the Americas they and their descendants were owned as property, worked under the whip, bought and sold, and denied schooling, marriage rights and family. Slavery ended in the British Empire in 1834–38, the United States in 1865 and Brazil, the last country in the Americas, in 1888.
US government writers interview over 2,300 formerly enslaved people.

Uprisings (Haiti, 1791–1804, the only successful slave revolution), escape networks such as the Underground Railroad, and abolition movements led partly by formerly enslaved people such as Frederick Douglass and Harriet Tubman.
About 1.8 million people died during the Middle Passage alone.
Whippings, rape, family separation and work until death; on Caribbean and Brazilian sugar plantations deaths were so high that planters relied on constant new arrivals from Africa.
Douglass, Equiano, Harriet Jacobs and the 1930s interviews describe beatings, sales of children and constant fear.
Old “Lost Cause” and apologist histories
The US House (2008) and Senate (2009) passed apologies; reparations are debated in the US, the UK and the Caribbean (CARICOM’s 10-point plan).

The Indian Removal Act of 1830 forced tens of thousands of Cherokee, Muscogee, Seminole, Chickasaw and Choctaw people from their homelands to land west of the Mississippi. On the Cherokee “Trail of Tears” (1838–39) about 4,000 of roughly 16,000 died. Wars, broken treaties, disease and the destruction of the buffalo followed across the West, ending at Wounded Knee in 1890.
Wounded Knee: US soldiers kill about 250–300 Lakota, many women and children.
Native resistance and legal battles continue, with wins such as McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020).
Loss of most of their land; tens of thousands of deaths from removal, war and disease; the near-extinction of the buffalo.
The treaties, the court rulings and the deaths.
Ethnic cleansing and, some argue, genocide.
Historians debate whether “genocide” applies to every case.
Native nations govern 574 federally recognized tribes; land, water and treaty disputes continue.

In the US and Canada, governments and churches removed Native children from their families to schools designed, in the words of a founder of the Carlisle school, to “kill the Indian … and save the man”. Children were punished for speaking their languages; many were abused; thousands died.
Canada’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission calls the system cultural genocide.
US Interior Department investigation finds at least 973 children died in federal boarding schools.
About 150,000 children passed through Canada’s schools; thousands died there; abuse and the loss of language and family harmed generations.
Searches for unmarked graves using ground-penetrating radar began in 2021; few sites have been excavated and some findings are debated.

King Leopold II of Belgium ruled the Congo as his private colony. To meet rubber quotas, his agents held women hostage, burned villages and cut off hands as proof of bullets used. Missionaries, journalists and the British consul Roger Casement exposed it; international outrage forced Belgium to take over in 1908.
Estimates of deaths range from about 1 to 10 million; mutilations, hostage-taking and forced labour were systematic.
One of the worst colonial atrocities; the death toll is disputed, the brutality is not.
In 2020 Belgium’s king expressed “deepest regrets”; there has been no formal apology or reparations.

In German South West Africa (now Namibia), the Herero rose against land seizures. General Lothar von Trotha issued an extermination order in 1904; survivors were driven into the desert to die of thirst or held in concentration camps. Historians call it the first genocide of the 20th century.
Germany acknowledges genocide and offers €1.1 billion in development aid.
About 65,000 of 80,000 Herero and about 10,000 of 20,000 Nama died (common estimates).
Genocide that deserves reparations, negotiated with them directly.
Many Herero and Nama leaders rejected the 2021 agreement as inadequate and negotiated without them.

Australian governments and missions removed Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families, aiming to assimilate them into white society. A national inquiry (Bringing Them Home, 1997) found that between one in ten and one in three Indigenous children were taken in this period.
Voters reject an Indigenous Voice to Parliament (about 60% No).
Survivors’ testimony to the inquiry; family-tracing services; the 2008 apology.
Meets the definition of genocide in international law, a finding still debated.

Repeated famines struck India under British rule. In 1876–78 and 1896–1902 millions died while grain was exported and relief was kept minimal. In 1943 about 3 million died in Bengal during the Second World War.
Amartya Sen shows famine can strike when food exists but people lose the means to buy it.
Independent India has had no famine of that scale since 1947; Sen links this to democracy and a free press.
Millions of deaths; families sold land and children to survive.
Drought and war made famine unavoidable.
Policy choices turned shortage into mass death.
Historians debate how much specific leaders, such as Churchill, were to blame in 1943.

On 6 and 9 August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. About 150,000–246,000 people died within months. Survivors, the hibakusha, faced burns, radiation sickness, cancer and discrimination, and became the world’s strongest voices against nuclear weapons.
Survivors’ testimony helped build the taboo against using nuclear weapons since 1945.
Mass death of civilians, including Korean forced labourers in the cities; lifelong illness.
The US has never apologized; President Obama visited Hiroshima in 2016.

Naval bases and coaling stations, markets in Asia, sugar planters’ interests, and a belief that Americans should “civilize” others.

The US entered WWI in 1917, became the world’s main creditor, and President Wilson proposed the League of Nations, which the Senate then refused to join.

Estimates of the US share of world output in 1945 vary (often put near half of world industrial production); it was a historic peak caused partly by the destruction of everyone else.

Aid came with politics: communists were expelled from the French and Italian governments in May 1947, just as US aid was being planned (historians debate how much US pressure caused it), and the CIA secretly funded Italy’s Christian Democrats in the 1948 election.
Western Europeans mostly asked for the US to stay (historian Geir Lundestad called it “empire by invitation”), and Western Europe became prosperous and democratic.
